old.title: Surgery after oligometastatic disease responds
old.question: When synchronous oligometastatic PDAC responds to chemotherapy, or isolated lung metastases appear late, should surgery be offered outside a trial?
old.status: Proposed; trial or registry first · OPEN proposal
old.proposal: Distant metastasis stays systemic-therapy-led. Response-selected conversion surgery for limited liver metastases is offered preferably within a trial (METAPANC, CSPAC-1) or a registry after MDT review. Metachronous isolated lung metastases after a long disease-free interval may be resected. There is no PDAC transplant pathway.
rules: Synchronous liver oligometastases: ≤3 liver metastases (OligoPanc working definition, relative-majority only; METAPANC ≤3 liver-only), no peritoneal or other extrahepatic disease, induction chemotherapy without progression (METAPANC: 8 cycles of mFOLFIRINOX; Heidelberg: usually ≥6 cycles with RECIST response of metastases and a marker fall), CA19-9 fall >50% to <500 U/mL (CSPAC-1), resectable primary and metastases.

Counsel: in Heidelberg, 46% were unresectable at exploration and only about 1 in 4 explored was ypM0; median survival 25.5 months (ypM0) vs 10.7 (ypM1) vs 8.1 (exploration only). Surgery ≥9 months after diagnosis did worse.
Metachronous isolated lung metastases: ≤3 (ideally solitary), unilateral, disease-free interval of about 2 years (17–28 months cited), after systemic therapy and MDT review.

Para-aortic (16b1) nodes known before surgery are systemic disease and outside the OligoPanc Delphi definition (although panellists rated a para-aortic nodal vignette as oligometastatic); when found at operation, do not abort resection on 16b1 alone.
old.rationale: Survival after resection is concentrated in complete responders, and unselected resection of metastases does not help. Trial rules give the clearest selection thresholds.

studies.population: Heidelberg, 173 explored after chemotherapy for metastatic PDAC. RECIST PR/CR of metastases plus a fall in CA19-9 and CEA, usually ≥6 cycles.
studies.results: 93 resected (45 ypM0); median survival 25.5 vs 10.7 vs 8.1 months; CA19-9 ≥400 HR 2.31; surgery ≥9 months after diagnosis HR 1.82.
studies.limits: Single referral centre; no intention-to-treat denominator.

studies.population: International Delphi consensus. ≤3 lesions in one organ (liver or lung) reached only relative majority (58% and 42%); systemic therapy before local treatment in synchronous disease (82%).
studies.results: No induction duration or response thresholds defined.

studies.population: METAPANC randomized trial protocol. ≤3 liver metastases, no extrahepatic disease; 8 cycles mFOLFIRINOX; CR, PR or stable disease randomized.
studies.results: No results yet.

studies.population: CSPAC-1 randomized trial protocol. ≤3 liver foci; randomization requires SD/PR and CA19-9 fall >50% to <500 U/mL.
studies.results: No results located.

studies.results: Surgery associated with longer survival (HR 0.41); the HR 0.18 figure is a model scenario, not an observed effect.

studies.results: Pooled HR 0.637 (0.531–0.764); significant publication bias; survival from pancreatectomy.

studies.results: Metastasectomy 33.0 vs 19.0 months (n=24, unadjusted).

studies.results: PDAC 16b1-positive median survival 10 vs 24 months (aHR 2.33); authors advise against aborting resection on 16b1 alone.

where.label: 3 · Resectable disease: surgery or neoadjuvant treatment

positions.says: Upfront surgery then postoperative therapy has been the standard; neoadjuvant therapy is permitted in resectable disease, especially with high-risk features, but evidence for specific regimens off-trial is limited. Either PREOPANC-2 regimen may be considered.
positions.locator: Gate 3 · Standard group · options 'Upfront resection, then adjuvant mFOLFIRINOX' and 'Neoadjuvant FOLFIRINOX, then surgery' (when); Reasonable 'Neoadjuvant chemotherapy for a resectable tumour that has high-risk features…'

positions.says: Recommends against neoadjuvant therapy for resectable disease outside clinical trials, citing limited phase III evidence [II, E]. The roadmap notes it predates PREOPANC-2, NORPACT-1 and the 2025 meta-analyses and describes no search strategy.
positions.locator: Gate 3 · Standard group · option 'Upfront resection, then adjuvant mFOLFIRINOX' (when); What we are not sure about · 'ESMO's 2023 guideline recommends against neoadjuvant therapy…'

positions.says: The only randomised trial of neoadjuvant FOLFIRINOX against upfront surgery restricted to resectable head cancer; its primary endpoint favoured upfront surgery (18-month survival 73% vs 60%). The roadmap reads it as no benefit shown: phase 2 at alpha 0.15, non-significant per protocol, and 21% of the neoadjuvant arm never received FOLFIRINOX and went straight to resection.
positions.locator: Gate 3 · Standard group · option 'Neoadjuvant FOLFIRINOX, then surgery' (avoid, note)

positions.says: Neoadjuvant gemcitabine chemoradiotherapy improved long-term survival (HR 0.73) in mixed resectable and borderline disease after a negative primary analysis; resectable subgroup non-significant (HR 0.79), and half the control arm received no chemotherapy.
positions.locator: Gate 3 · Standard group · option 'Neoadjuvant gemcitabine-based chemoradiotherapy, then surgery, then adjuvant gemcitabine' (when, avoid, note)

positions.says: Neoadjuvant FOLFIRINOX without adjuvant therapy and the PREOPANC chemoradiotherapy regimen gave similar survival (21.9 vs 21.3 months, HR 0.88), with no upfront-surgery arm; the roadmap calls it a failed superiority trial that justifies FOLFIRINOX if neoadjuvant.

old.divergence: NCCN permits and ESMO advises against neoadjuvant therapy in resectable disease; NORPACT-1 pointed to upfront surgery and PREOPANC to neoadjuvant treatment in a mixed population, the pooled resectable subgroup shows no benefit (HR 0.90), and no trial has tested the comparator with adjuvant mFOLFIRINOX.
old.proposal: The roadmap lists upfront resection then adjuvant mFOLFIRINOX first for fit patients without high-risk features, as what randomised evidence supports, while saying it does not resolve the question. If a neoadjuvant route is chosen - for named high-risk features, or where the board judges selecting out occult metastatic disease worth the resection-rate cost - tissue comes first and the regimen is FOLFIRINOX, or PREOPANC chemoradiotherapy if FOLFIRINOX is not tolerable; offer a randomised trial where one is recruiting (A021806 is active but not recruiting).
old.proposal_locator: Gate 3 · Standard group (order note, flagnote and options); Reasonable 'Neoadjuvant chemotherapy for a resectable tumour that has high-risk features…'; Avoid 'Do not start neoadjuvant therapy without a tissue diagnosis.'
old.rationale: The trials disagree and the page does not resolve them, and the full-text read made the disagreement worse rather than better. No neoadjuvant trial gave its control arm modern adjuvant therapy except NORPACT-1, and there only 19 of 44 resected control patients (43%) received adjuvant mFOLFIRINOX; PREOPANC's control arm received adjuvant gemcitabine and only 51% of it received any chemotherapy; PREOPANC-2 has no upfront-surgery arm; S1505 and A021501 had no randomised control at all. Pooled across nine randomised trials the resectable subgroup shows no benefit (HR 0.90, 0.63–1.28) and the borderline resectable subgroup does (HR 0.60, 0.38–0.96), but the between-subgroup test is not significant (p=0.081) and the pooled estimate depends on post hoc removal of NORPACT-1. NORPACT-1's primary endpoint favoured upfront surgery at a two-sided alpha of 0.15, was non-significant per protocol, and had 21% of its neoadjuvant arm go straight to resection without the drug. ESMO recommends against neoadjuvant therapy in resectable disease at [II, E]. The pooled data also show no gain in adjuvant initiation (57.7% versus 55.6%, p=0.353), which removes the main mechanistic argument. A021806 has not reported. This has to be a local decision because there is no guideline answer to copy and no trial of the comparison that matters.
old.audit: Registry: resectability category, sequence chosen, resection rate, R0 rate, time from diagnosis to first treatment, and proportion of resected patients who never start adjuvant therapy.

old.divergence: ESMO ranks mFOLFIRINOX first for fit patients and names criteria for the doublet, whereas NCCN lists both as preferred without ranking them; PRODIGE 24's restricted eligibility leaves the unrecovered or older patient undefined, and the two regimens were never compared.
old.proposal: mFOLFIRINOX for 24 weeks is listed first for a recovered patient with good performance status; gemcitabine with capecitabine for a patient who cannot take a triplet (poorer performance status, neuropathy, slow recovery or preference); gemcitabine alone for the frail. No numeric switch threshold is stated; restage before the first cycle and prioritise completing the course.
old.proposal_locator: Gate 6 · Standard group · options (pref); Standard 'Restage before the first cycle…'; Standard 'Prioritise completing the course over starting it quickly.'
old.rationale: On mature 5-year data PRODIGE 24 gives median overall survival 53.5 versus 35.5 months and 5-year survival 43.2% versus 31.4%, at the cost of grade 3–4 adverse events in 75.9% versus 52.9%, in a trial restricted to age under 80, no symptomatic heart failure or coronary artery disease, WHO performance status 0–1, full surgical recovery and postoperative CA 19-9 of 180 U/mL or less. The effect attenuated from the 3-year report (DFS HR 0.58 to 0.66, OS 0.64 to 0.68), 5-year disease-free survival differs by only 7.1 points, only 33.6% of patients achieved a relative dose intensity of 0.80 or more, post-relapse survival was numerically worse in the mFOLFIRINOX arm (13.1 versus 15.0 months) with fewer of its relapsing patients receiving any chemotherapy (66.9% versus 83.0%), and in the 101 patients aged 70 or older the benefit did not reach significance (HR 0.86, 0.53–1.39). Nothing in it describes the patient who has not recovered from a pancreatoduodenectomy, which is a substantial fraction of the real population, and quality of life was never collected.
old.audit: Registry: adjuvant regimen, cycles completed, dose intensity, grade 3–4 toxicity, time from surgery to first cycle.

positions.says: After gemcitabine-based induction, adding chemoradiotherapy did not improve survival (HR 1.03; stopped for futility, underpowered) but reduced locoregional progression (32% vs 46%); 18% of radiotherapy plans had major deviations.

positions.says: After mostly FOLFIRINOX induction, chemoradiotherapy did not improve survival (HR 0.937) and missed its R0 endpoint (25% vs 18%), which was rewritten mid-trial; R0 gain only among operated patients; locoregional recurrence HR 0.33.

old.divergence: Both randomised trials are null for survival and both show better local control; neither tested radiotherapy after FOLFIRINOX with modern surgery and adjuvant therapy, so the choice turns on the objective rather than on evidence.
old.proposal: Continue chemotherapy alone after induction as the default where the objective is survival; offer chemoradiotherapy only where the board's stated objective is local control or a clear margin in a responder heading to surgery, recording which; never present radiotherapy as survival-prolonging. Upfront radiotherapy without induction is reserved for a narrow group.
old.proposal_locator: Gate 7 · Reasonable group (order note and options); Gate 7 · Avoid 'Do not offer radiotherapy as a survival-prolonging treatment in locally advanced disease.'
old.rationale: LAP07 (HR 1.03, P=.83, stopped at interim for futility with that analysis declared final, 18% major radiotherapy protocol deviations, survival measured from the first of two randomisations) and CONKO-007 (HR 0.937, P=.57, primary endpoint not met at 25% versus 18% R0) are both null for overall survival. CONKO-007's primary endpoint was changed mid-trial from overall survival to R0 rate with the new effect size calculated from its own unblinded interim data on 180 already-enrolled patients, its radiotherapy was never centrally reviewed for stated financial reasons, and its significant R0 advantage (69.4% versus 50.0%) is confined to patients who reached theatre, which was not randomised. What both trials do show is better local control (CONKO-007 locoregional recurrence HR 0.33, 0.206–0.530, P<.001; LAP07 32% versus 46%, P=.03). Neither tested radiotherapy after a FOLFIRINOX backbone followed by modern surgery and modern adjuvant therapy, so the local position has to be a judgement about objectives rather than a reading of evidence.
old.audit: Registry: induction regimen, radiation given or not, proportion reaching exploration, R0 rate, local progression, overall survival from the start of induction.

Daraxonrasib is listed first among later-line options for a previously treated patient with a documented RAS G12 mutation, after checking availability, regulatory status and coverage; its place relative to other second-line regimens is not set.

old.rationale: The commonest failure in metastatic PDAC is a genomic report that arrives after the patient is too unwell to act on it, which is an operational problem with a named-owner solution. The sequencing question is separate: RASolute 302 is a phase 3 result with dual primary endpoints met in the RAS G12 population (median overall survival 13.2 versus 6.6 months, HR 0.40; progression-free survival 7.3 versus 3.5 months, HR 0.45), and benefit was also demonstrated in the overall population; the non-G12 subgroup was small and exploratory (n=41; PFS HR 1.38, 0.60–3.17; OS HR 0.37, 0.15–0.93), 38 of 252 patients (15.1%) allocated to the comparator never received it against 7 of 248 (2.8%) on daraxonrasib, and the comparator was unconstrained investigator's choice with a 6.6-month median at the low end of published second-line outcomes. The local position depends on availability, regulatory status and cost, and should state which RAS alterations it covers. [PAYER]

old.proposal: Drain before neoadjuvant therapy with an endoscopic self-expanding metal stent placed in the same anaesthetic as the EUS biopsy: fully covered while the diagnosis is uncertain, partially covered or bare once confirmed, as short as feasible; plastic only for palliation under 3 months. Expected duration, re-imaging responsibility and ownership of unresolved jaundice are not stated.
old.proposal_locator: Gate 2 · Standard 'Where the patient is jaundiced and needs tissue…'; Standard 'Biliary drainage is not routinely recommended…'; Standard 'Choose the stent for the diagnostic state…'
old.rationale: The only randomised trial of preoperative drainage used plastic stents for 4 to 6 weeks, capped bilirubin at 250 micromol/L, excluded neoadjuvant chemotherapy by protocol, and required an operation within one week in its control arm, guaranteed by dedicated theatre capacity at all 13 hospitals. It showed that the drainage strategy caused more complications overall (74% versus 39%) while surgical complications did not differ (37% versus 47%, RR 0.79, 0.57–1.11), so it says nothing about bridging a patient through months of preoperative treatment. That situation is where drainage is now most often needed and where it most often derails treatment: NORPACT-1 stented 57% of its neoadjuvant arm against 16% of the surgery arm, and two of the 16 patients who never received neoadjuvant FOLFIRINOX were lost to persistent jaundice after stenting and two to biliary infection; PREOPANC had 10 patients whose treatment was delayed by persistent jaundice.
old.audit: Registry: stent type by diagnostic certainty, time from stent to first cycle, cholangitis and re-intervention rate, and treatment delays or non-receipt attributable to jaundice.

The survival advantage of surgery within that trial (HR 0.525, 0.408–0.676) is a non-randomised comparison of operated with non-operated patients. LAP07, from gemcitabine-based induction, reached resection in 18 of 442 patients (4%). The 159 of 495 patients (32.1%) who progressed during induction had a median survival of 9 months with no 5-year survivors. The group must decide whether it offers this at all, to whom, and with what number on the consent form.

Also require a contemporary comparator or credible comparative design, immunosuppression/drug-safety evaluation, and independent transplant, pancreatic oncology, methods, ethics, donor and allocation approval with funded oversight.

new.title: Surgery after oligometastatic disease responds
new.question: When synchronous oligometastatic PDAC responds to chemotherapy, or isolated lung metastases appear late, should surgery be offered outside a trial?
new.status: Proposed; trial or registry first · OPEN proposal
new.proposal: Distant metastasis stays systemic-therapy-led. Response-selected conversion surgery for limited liver metastases is offered preferably within a trial (METAPANC, CSPAC-1) or a registry after MDT review. Metachronous isolated lung metastases after a long disease-free interval may be resected. There is no PDAC transplant pathway.
rules: Synchronous liver oligometastases: ≤3 liver metastases (OligoPanc working definition, relative-majority only; METAPANC ≤3 liver-only), no peritoneal or other extrahepatic disease, induction chemotherapy without progression (METAPANC: 8 cycles of mFOLFIRINOX; Heidelberg: usually ≥6 cycles with RECIST response of metastases and a marker fall), CA19-9 fall >50% to <500 U/mL (CSPAC-1), resectable primary and metastases.

Counsel: in Heidelberg, 46% were unresectable at exploration and only about 1 in 4 explored was ypM0; median survival 25.5 months (ypM0) vs 10.7 (ypM1) vs 8.1 (exploration only). Surgery ≥9 months after diagnosis did worse.
Metachronous isolated lung metastases: ≤3 (ideally solitary), unilateral, disease-free interval of about 2 years (17–28 months cited), after systemic therapy and MDT review.

Para-aortic (16b1) nodes known before surgery are systemic disease and outside the OligoPanc Delphi definition (although panellists rated a para-aortic nodal vignette as oligometastatic); when found at operation, do not abort resection on 16b1 alone.
new.rationale: Survival after resection is concentrated in complete responders, and unselected resection of metastases does not help. Trial rules give the clearest selection thresholds.

studies.population: Heidelberg, 173 explored after chemotherapy for metastatic PDAC. RECIST PR/CR of metastases plus a fall in CA19-9 and CEA, usually ≥6 cycles.
studies.results: 93 resected (45 ypM0); median survival 25.5 vs 10.7 vs 8.1 months; CA19-9 ≥400 HR 2.31; surgery ≥9 months after diagnosis HR 1.82.
studies.limits: Single referral centre; no intention-to-treat denominator.

studies.population: International Delphi consensus. ≤3 lesions in one organ (liver or lung) reached only relative majority (58% and 42%); systemic therapy before local treatment in synchronous disease (82%).
studies.results: No induction duration or response thresholds defined.

studies.results: No results yet.

studies.results: No results located.

studies.results: Surgery associated with longer survival (HR 0.41); the HR 0.18 figure is a model scenario, not an observed effect.
studies.limits: Retrospective; misattributed coefficient in the abstract.

studies.results: Pooled HR 0.637 (0.531–0.764); significant publication bias; survival from pancreatectomy.

studies.results: Metastasectomy 33.0 vs 19.0 months (n=24, unadjusted).

studies.results: PDAC 16b1-positive median survival 10 vs 24 months (aHR 2.33); authors advise against aborting resection on 16b1 alone.

positions.says: The only randomised trial of neoadjuvant FOLFIRINOX against upfront surgery restricted to resectable head cancer; its primary endpoint favoured upfront surgery (18-month survival 73% vs 60%). The roadmap reads it as no benefit shown: phase 2 at alpha 0.15, non-significant per protocol, and 21% of the neoadjuvant arm never received FOLFIRINOX and went straight to resection.

positions.says: Neoadjuvant FOLFIRINOX without adjuvant therapy and the PREOPANC chemoradiotherapy regimen gave similar survival (21.9 vs 21.3 months, HR 0.88), with no upfront-surgery arm; the roadmap calls it a failed superiority trial that justifies FOLFIRINOX if neoadjuvant.
positions.locator: Gate 3 · Standard group · option 'Neoadjuvant FOLFIRINOX, then surgery' (when, pref)

new.divergence: NCCN permits and ESMO advises against neoadjuvant therapy in resectable disease; NORPACT-1 pointed to upfront surgery and PREOPANC to neoadjuvant treatment in a mixed population, the pooled resectable subgroup shows no benefit (HR 0.90), and no trial has tested the comparator with adjuvant mFOLFIRINOX.
new.proposal: The roadmap lists upfront resection then adjuvant mFOLFIRINOX first for fit patients without high-risk features, as what randomised evidence supports, while saying it does not resolve the question. If a neoadjuvant route is chosen - for named high-risk features, or where the board judges selecting out occult metastatic disease worth the resection-rate cost - tissue comes first and the regimen is FOLFIRINOX, or PREOPANC chemoradiotherapy if FOLFIRINOX is not tolerable; offer a randomised trial where one is recruiting (A021806 is active but not recruiting).
new.proposal_locator: Gate 3 · Standard group (order note, flagnote and options); Reasonable 'Neoadjuvant chemotherapy for a resectable tumour that has high-risk features…'; Avoid 'Do not start neoadjuvant therapy without a tissue diagnosis.'
new.rationale: The trials disagree and the page does not resolve them, and the full-text read made the disagreement worse rather than better. No neoadjuvant trial gave its control arm modern adjuvant therapy except NORPACT-1, and there only 19 of 44 resected control patients (43%) received adjuvant mFOLFIRINOX; PREOPANC's control arm received adjuvant gemcitabine and only 51% of it received any chemotherapy; PREOPANC-2 has no upfront-surgery arm; S1505 and A021501 had no randomised control at all. Pooled across nine randomised trials the resectable subgroup shows no benefit (HR 0.90, 0.63–1.28) and the borderline resectable subgroup does (HR 0.60, 0.38–0.96), but the between-subgroup test is not significant (p=0.081) and the pooled estimate depends on post hoc removal of NORPACT-1. NORPACT-1's primary endpoint favoured upfront surgery at a two-sided alpha of 0.15, was non-significant per protocol, and had 21% of its neoadjuvant arm go straight to resection without the drug. ESMO recommends against neoadjuvant therapy in resectable disease at [II, E]. The pooled data also show no gain in adjuvant initiation (57.7% versus 55.6%, p=0.353), which removes the main mechanistic argument. A021806 has not reported. This has to be a local decision because there is no guideline answer to copy and no trial of the comparison that matters.
new.audit: Registry: resectability category, sequence chosen, resection rate, R0 rate, time from diagnosis to first treatment, and proportion of resected patients who never start adjuvant therapy.

No numeric switch threshold is stated; restage before the first cycle and prioritise completing the course.

new.rationale: On mature 5-year data PRODIGE 24 gives median overall survival 53.5 versus 35.5 months and 5-year survival 43.2% versus 31.4%, at the cost of grade 3–4 adverse events in 75.9% versus 52.9%, in a trial restricted to age under 80, no symptomatic heart failure or coronary artery disease, WHO performance status 0–1, full surgical recovery and postoperative CA 19-9 of 180 U/mL or less. The effect attenuated from the 3-year report (DFS HR 0.58 to 0.66, OS 0.64 to 0.68), 5-year disease-free survival differs by only 7.1 points, only 33.6% of patients achieved a relative dose intensity of 0.80 or more, post-relapse survival was numerically worse in the mFOLFIRINOX arm (13.1 versus 15.0 months) with fewer of its relapsing patients receiving any chemotherapy (66.9% versus 83.0%), and in the 101 patients aged 70 or older the benefit did not reach significance (HR 0.86, 0.53–1.39). Nothing in it describes the patient who has not recovered from a pancreatoduodenectomy, which is a substantial fraction of the real population, and quality of life was never collected.

Its systemic matrix only advises planning about six months of adjuvant mFOLFIRINOX adjusted for prior neoadjuvant exposure and recovery, and Gate 6 requires the neoadjuvant response to be known before adjuvant therapy starts.

new.title: Is consolidative chemoradiotherapy after induction therapy in locally advanced disease offered routinely, only where conversion to resection is the stated objective, or not at all?
new.question: Is consolidative chemoradiotherapy after induction therapy in locally advanced disease offered routinely, only where conversion to resection is the stated objective, or not at all?

where.label: 7 · Locally advanced disease: treatment and reassessment

positions.says: After gemcitabine-based induction, adding chemoradiotherapy did not improve survival (HR 1.03; stopped for futility, underpowered) but reduced locoregional progression (32% vs 46%); 18% of radiotherapy plans had major deviations.
positions.locator: Gate 7 · Reasonable group · option 'Continue chemotherapy alone after induction' (when, avoid, note)

positions.says: After mostly FOLFIRINOX induction, chemoradiotherapy did not improve survival (HR 0.937) and missed its R0 endpoint (25% vs 18%), which was rewritten mid-trial; R0 gain only among operated patients; locoregional recurrence HR 0.33.
positions.locator: Gate 7 · Reasonable group · option 'Chemoradiotherapy after induction, for local control or to raise the chance of R0' (when, pref, avoid, note)

positions.says: In single-arm cohorts a pooled 63.5% received radiotherapy, yet survival did not correlate with radiotherapy use (p=0.12); the authors say it remains unestablished who benefits from radiotherapy afterwards.
positions.locator: Gate 7 · Standard 'Multiagent induction chemotherapy…' (avoid, note)

new.divergence: Both randomised trials are null for survival and both show better local control; neither tested radiotherapy after FOLFIRINOX with modern surgery and adjuvant therapy, so the choice turns on the objective rather than on evidence.
new.proposal: Continue chemotherapy alone after induction as the default where the objective is survival; offer chemoradiotherapy only where the board's stated objective is local control or a clear margin in a responder heading to surgery, recording which; never present radiotherapy as survival-prolonging. Upfront radiotherapy without induction is reserved for a narrow group.
new.proposal_locator: Gate 7 · Reasonable group (order note and options); Gate 7 · Avoid 'Do not offer radiotherapy as a survival-prolonging treatment in locally advanced disease.'
new.rationale: LAP07 (HR 1.03, P=.83, stopped at interim for futility with that analysis declared final, 18% major radiotherapy protocol deviations, survival measured from the first of two randomisations) and CONKO-007 (HR 0.937, P=.57, primary endpoint not met at 25% versus 18% R0) are both null for overall survival. CONKO-007's primary endpoint was changed mid-trial from overall survival to R0 rate with the new effect size calculated from its own unblinded interim data on 180 already-enrolled patients, its radiotherapy was never centrally reviewed for stated financial reasons, and its significant R0 advantage (69.4% versus 50.0%) is confined to patients who reached theatre, which was not randomised. What both trials do show is better local control (CONKO-007 locoregional recurrence HR 0.33, 0.206–0.530, P<.001; LAP07 32% versus 46%, P=.03). Neither tested radiotherapy after a FOLFIRINOX backbone followed by modern surgery and modern adjuvant therapy, so the local position has to be a judgement about objectives rather than a reading of evidence.
new.audit: Registry: induction regimen, radiation given or not, proportion reaching exploration, R0 rate, local progression, overall survival from the start of induction.

new.title: Which triplet is the local first-line standard in metastatic disease — (m)FOLFIRINOX or NALIRIFOX — and what counts locally as good biliary drainage and adequate nutritional intake?
new.question: Which triplet is the local first-line standard in metastatic disease — (m)FOLFIRINOX or NALIRIFOX — and what counts locally as good biliary drainage and adequate nutritional intake?

where.label: 7 · Locally advanced disease: treatment and reassessment
8 · Metastatic disease: systemic treatment

positions.says: FOLFIRINOX improved median survival over gemcitabine (11.1 vs 6.8 months, HR 0.57) in ECOG 0–1 patients under 76 with bilirubin up to 1.5 times normal; the only first-line triplet with quality-of-life data.
positions.locator: Gate 8 · Standard group · option 'FOLFIRINOX or mFOLFIRINOX' (when, pref, avoid)

positions.says: NALIRIFOX beat nab-paclitaxel with gemcitabine (11.1 vs 9.2 months, HR 0.83) narrowly against its design threshold, with grade 3+ events 87% vs 86%, hierarchical testing broken at response rate, and no quality-of-life or cost data.
positions.locator: Gate 8 · Standard group · option 'NALIRIFOX' (when, avoid, note)

positions.says: States NALIRIFOX does not appear to have clear advantages over FOLFIRINOX or mFOLFIRINOX; defines eligibility for intensive therapy as ECOG 0–1 with good biliary drainage and adequate nutritional intake.
positions.locator: Gate 8 · Standard group · option 'NALIRIFOX' (avoid) and group flagnote

new.divergence: There is no randomised comparison of the two triplets, which share an 11.1-month median against different comparators in differently selected populations, and NCCN's drainage and nutrition terms are neither defined nor recorded locally.
new.proposal: The roadmap lists (m)FOLFIRINOX first and NALIRIFOX as an alternative for the same population when its schedule is preferred on toxicity or logistics, without naming a local standard. It adopts NCCN's eligibility wording, and its matrix asks for controlled biliary obstruction and adequate hepatic function, but drainage and nutrition are not defined.
new.proposal_locator: Gate 8 · Standard group (order note; options 'FOLFIRINOX or mFOLFIRINOX' and 'NALIRIFOX'); Systemic treatment matrix (v16 extract) row 'FOLFIRINOX or NALIRIFOX · Metastatic first line'
new.rationale: The two triplets sit at the same median overall survival (11.1 months) against different comparators in different eras, there is no randomised comparison between them, and NCCN states NALIRIFOX does not appear to have clear advantages over FOLFIRINOX or mFOLFIRINOX. The second half matters as much: NCCN's eligibility definition for intensive therapy is ECOG 0–1 with good biliary drainage and adequate nutritional intake, and the latter two are not currently recorded in a way that can be audited. [PAYER]
new.audit: Registry: first-line regimen, performance status, drainage and nutritional status at start, dose intensity, reason for discontinuation.

new.title: Who owns chasing the molecular report, and where does daraxonrasib sit in the local second-line sequence?
new.question: Who owns chasing the molecular report, and where does daraxonrasib sit in the local second-line sequence?

where.label: 8 · Metastatic disease: systemic treatment

positions.says: In previously treated RAS G12 disease daraxonrasib doubled median survival (13.2 vs 6.6 months, HR 0.40); non-G12 HR 1.38 (0.60–3.17); 15.1% of the chemotherapy arm never received it, which the roadmap says inflates the effect.
positions.locator: Gate 8 · Reasonable group · option 'Daraxonrasib for eligible metastatic PDAC; the US indication is not restricted to a RAS mutation' (when, pref, avoid, note)

positions.says: Per the roadmap's matrix, approved August 2026 after at least one prior systemic treatment or when multiagent therapy is unsuitable, not restricted to RAS mutation; the trial does not establish effect in treatment-naive frail patients.
positions.locator: Systemic treatment matrix (v16 extract) row 'Daraxonrasib · Current US option'; References

positions.says: Liposomal irinotecan with fluorouracil after gemcitabine improved survival (6.1 vs 4.2 months, HR 0.67); the roadmap notes no validated immediate reuse after FOLFIRINOX or NALIRIFOX.
positions.locator: Supporting study appraisals (v16 extract) · 'NAPOLI-1: nal-IRI after gemcitabine'; Systemic treatment matrix row 'Liposomal irinotecan … Subsequent treatment'

positions.says: Asks for comprehensive genomic profiling, germline testing and HER2 testing in every metastatic patient with tissue banked at biopsy, but treatment should not wait for the BRCA result.
positions.locator: Gate 8 · Standard 'Order comprehensive genomic profiling and germline testing at the first visit…' (pref, avoid)

new.divergence: RASolute 302 demonstrated benefit in both RAS G12 and the overall previously treated population; the US indication also includes patients unable to receive multiagent therapy, and the roadmap leaves daraxonrasib's place against other second-line options to availability, regulatory status and cost.
new.proposal: Order profiling at the first visit, bank extra passes at biopsy, and have medical oncology name the person who chases the result. Daraxonrasib is listed first among later-line options for a previously treated patient with a documented RAS G12 mutation, after checking availability, regulatory status and coverage; its place relative to other second-line regimens is not set.
new.proposal_locator: Operations · board meeting 'Molecular' step; Gate 8 · Avoid 'Do not let the molecular report arrive after it can be used.'; Gate 8 · Reasonable group · option 'Daraxonrasib…' (pref, avoid) and flagnote
new.rationale: The commonest failure in metastatic PDAC is a genomic report that arrives after the patient is too unwell to act on it, which is an operational problem with a named-owner solution. The sequencing question is separate: RASolute 302 is a phase 3 result with dual primary endpoints met in the RAS G12 population (median overall survival 13.2 versus 6.6 months, HR 0.40; progression-free survival 7.3 versus 3.5 months, HR 0.45), and benefit was also demonstrated in the overall population; the non-G12 subgroup was small and exploratory (n=41; PFS HR 1.38, 0.60–3.17; OS HR 0.37, 0.15–0.93), 38 of 252 patients (15.1%) allocated to the comparator never received it against 7 of 248 (2.8%) on daraxonrasib, and the comparator was unconstrained investigator's choice with a 6.6-month median at the low end of published second-line outcomes. The local position depends on availability, regulatory status and cost, and should state which RAS alterations it covers. [PAYER]
new.audit: Registry: proportion with completed germline and genomic results before second line, time from biopsy to report, proportion of actionable results acted on, second-line agent.

new.title: What is the surveillance schedule after resection, and who owns the NCCN update check?
new.question: What is the surveillance schedule after resection, and who owns the NCCN update check?

where.label: 6 · Adjuvant therapy and surveillance

positions.says: Offers post-resection surveillance (history, CA 19-9, contrast CT) on consensus that earlier detection may allow trial entry; CA 19-9 is category 2B, and rising markers or serial ctDNA have no outcome evidence. The interval footnote was lost in extraction.
positions.locator: Gate 6 · Reasonable 'Surveillance after resection…' (pref, avoid, note); References · nonpm 'NCCN pancreatic adenocarcinoma'

positions.says: Regular surveillance CT showed no significant survival benefit.
positions.locator: Gate 6 · Reasonable 'Surveillance after resection…' (avoid)

new.divergence: NCCN offers surveillance on consensus grounds while the only outcome data quoted are negative, and its interval could not be read from the extraction.
new.proposal: The roadmap offers surveillance (history and examination, CA 19-9, contrast CT of abdomen and pelvis) with an explicit statement of what it is for, quotes no interval, and asks that the interval be confirmed against the current published guideline with the version recorded. No owner for guideline update checks is named.
new.proposal_locator: Gate 6 · Reasonable 'Surveillance after resection…' (t, note); What we are not sure about · 'The surveillance schedule after resection is not stated…'; Operations · dashboard 'Source currency…'
new.rationale: The guideline footnote defining the surveillance interval did not survive the machine extraction supplied to this page, so no interval is quoted here. What is known is that regular surveillance CT showed no significant survival benefit in a SEER-Medicare analysis, CA 19-9 is category 2B, and serial ctDNA monitoring has no evidence of benefit — so the interval is a local choice about what surveillance is for. Separately, every numeric criterion on this page needs an owner for re-verification against the next guideline edition.
new.audit: Named owner plus edition and date, with an agreed update cycle; surveillance interval recorded and adherence audited once set.

new.title: Who adjudicates the resectability category before it is used to route a patient, given that roughly a third of patients called resectable by their own centres do not meet the criteria?
new.question: Who adjudicates the resectability category before it is used to route a patient, given that roughly a third of patients called resectable by their own centres do not meet the criteria?

where.label: 1 · Classify resectability

positions.says: Resectability status should be decided by consensus at multidisciplinary meetings; the resectable criteria deliberately favour specificity over sensitivity so that no potentially resectable patient is denied an operation.
positions.locator: Gate 1 · Standard 'Place the patient in exactly one of resectable, borderline resectable…' (pref, avoid); Quick reference · 'Resectability criteria at diagnosis' (foot)

positions.says: Read the NCCN anatomical criteria alongside the International Association of Pancreatology biological and conditional features [III, B], with board discussion in an expert centre [III, A].
positions.locator: Gate 1 · Standard 'Place the patient in exactly one of…' (pref)

positions.says: Despite protocol scans and surgical consultation at experienced centres, central review found 29% (43 of 146) of patients called resectable did not meet the criteria; a site radiologist checklist lowered this only from 33% to 26%.
positions.locator: Gate 1 · Standard 'Place the patient in exactly one of…' (note); What we are not sure about · 'Roughly a third of patients called resectable are not…'

positions.says: Adopted rather than derived the 180-degree threshold, with no inter-reader reproducibility data for measuring circumferential contact and no validation that using the template changes decisions.
positions.locator: Gate 1 · Standard 'Place the patient in exactly one of…' (avoid); What we are not sure about · 'The resectability thresholds are a shared language…'

new.divergence: Guidelines require multidisciplinary consensus but specify no independent read, while S1505 shows substantial misclassification despite checklists and the thresholds lack reproducibility data.
new.proposal: A named reader checks the degrees of arterial and venous contact against the images at triage before listing; the category is then assigned by consensus in the meeting and recorded with degrees, date and the names of those agreeing, owned by the chair. Whether a second independent read, radiology-lead sign-off or external review is required is left open.
new.proposal_locator: Operations · board meeting 'Triage' and 'Resectability call' steps; Gate 1 · Avoid 'Do not close the case on one radiologist's word unresectable.'
new.rationale: In SWOG S1505, at experienced US trial centres with a mandatory pancreas-protocol scan within 28 days and formal surgical consultation within 21 days, central radiology review found 43 of 146 patients (29%) did not meet the resectability criteria — 51% with arterial interface, 35% with venous interface of 180 degrees or more, 65% with suspicion of distant disease — and all had already started protocol therapy. A site radiologist checklist moved the rate only from 33% to 26%. The category decides which assessment on this page a patient enters, so the group must decide whether a second independent read, a radiology lead sign-off or an external review is required, and for which categories.
new.audit: Registry: proportion of cases where the board's category differed from the referring report, by referring source; proportion of operations abandoned at exploration for disease more advanced than imaging suggested.

new.title: What is the local rule for biliary drainage in a patient going on to neoadjuvant therapy — stent type, expected duration, who re-images and who owns the jaundice if it does not settle?
new.question: What is the local rule for biliary drainage in a patient going on to neoadjuvant therapy — stent type, expected duration, who re-images and who owns the jaundice if it does not settle?

where.label: 2 · Plan tissue sampling and biliary drainage

positions.says: Routine plastic-stent drainage before early surgery raised serious complications (74% vs 39%) without changing surgical complications; it excluded neoadjuvant chemotherapy, capped bilirubin at 250 µmol/L and required surgery within a week.
positions.locator: Gate 2 · Standard 'Biliary drainage is not routinely recommended before an operation…' (avoid, note); What we are not sure about · 'The DROP trial does not say…'

positions.says: Decompression is necessary before neoadjuvant therapy and is best done with an endoscopic stent; it calls stents an evolving technology, notes covered stents may migrate, and sees no obvious differences between covered and uncovered stents.
positions.locator: Gate 2 · Standard 'Biliary drainage is not routinely recommended…' (pref); Standard 'Choose the stent for the diagnostic state…' (note)

positions.says: Recommends endoscopic drainage when bilirubin exceeds 250 µmol/L with cholangitis, planned neoadjuvant treatment, or surgery delayed beyond 2 weeks [I, B].
positions.locator: Gate 2 · Standard 'Biliary drainage is not routinely recommended…' (pref)

positions.says: Stented 57% of its neoadjuvant arm versus 16% of the surgery arm; of 16 patients who never received FOLFIRINOX, two were lost to persistent jaundice after stenting and two to biliary infection.
positions.locator: Decisions this programme still has to make · item 13 (why)

new.divergence: The only randomised trial excluded neoadjuvant therapy and tested plastic stents, the preference for metal stents rests on practice rather than comparison, and no source addresses bridging a patient through months of preoperative treatment.
new.proposal: Drain before neoadjuvant therapy with an endoscopic self-expanding metal stent placed in the same anaesthetic as the EUS biopsy: fully covered while the diagnosis is uncertain, partially covered or bare once confirmed, as short as feasible; plastic only for palliation under 3 months. Expected duration, re-imaging responsibility and ownership of unresolved jaundice are not stated.
new.proposal_locator: Gate 2 · Standard 'Where the patient is jaundiced and needs tissue…'; Standard 'Biliary drainage is not routinely recommended…'; Standard 'Choose the stent for the diagnostic state…'
new.rationale: The only randomised trial of preoperative drainage used plastic stents for 4 to 6 weeks, capped bilirubin at 250 micromol/L, excluded neoadjuvant chemotherapy by protocol, and required an operation within one week in its control arm, guaranteed by dedicated theatre capacity at all 13 hospitals. It showed that the drainage strategy caused more complications overall (74% versus 39%) while surgical complications did not differ (37% versus 47%, RR 0.79, 0.57–1.11), so it says nothing about bridging a patient through months of preoperative treatment. That situation is where drainage is now most often needed and where it most often derails treatment: NORPACT-1 stented 57% of its neoadjuvant arm against 16% of the surgery arm, and two of the 16 patients who never received neoadjuvant FOLFIRINOX were lost to persistent jaundice after stenting and two to biliary infection; PREOPANC had 10 patients whose treatment was delayed by persistent jaundice.
new.audit: Registry: stent type by diagnostic certainty, time from stent to first cycle, cholangitis and re-intervention rate, and treatment delays or non-receipt attributable to jaundice.

new.title: Does this programme offer conversion surgery after induction therapy in locally advanced disease, and what operative mortality is quoted in the consent conversation?
new.question: Does this programme offer conversion surgery after induction therapy in locally advanced disease, and what operative mortality is quoted in the consent conversation?

where.label: 7 · Locally advanced disease: treatment and reassessment

positions.says: Of 336 patients randomised after induction without progression, 36–37% reached theatre and 22% achieved R0; 30-day postoperative mortality was 8% in both arms, and the survival advantage of surgery is a non-randomised comparison.
positions.locator: Gate 7 · Standard 'Offer conversion surgery only where R0 is achievable…' (note); Avoid 'Do not promise an operation at the start of induction therapy.'

positions.says: Gemcitabine-based induction led to curative-intent resection in only 18 of 442 patients (4%).
positions.locator: Gate 7 · Reasonable group · option 'Continue chemotherapy alone after induction' (note)

positions.says: Single-arm cohorts report pooled resection in 25.9%, and R0 in 78.4% of resected patients with margin data (60 of 81, about 19% of the cohort), with survival measured from the start of FOLFIRINOX and no control group.
positions.locator: Gate 7 · Standard 'Multiagent induction chemotherapy…' (pref, avoid)

positions.says: Use locally advanced only at diagnosis; base resection after neoadjuvant therapy on biological response; refer responders for a second opinion at a vascular-resection centre; restrict arterial resection, with counselling that the benefit is unknown.
positions.locator: Gate 7 · Standard 'Re-ask the resectability question on biological response…' (pref); Standard 'Offer conversion surgery only where R0 is achievable…' (avoid)

new.divergence: Conversion ranges from 4% after gemcitabine induction to roughly a quarter to a third after FOLFIRINOX-based induction, the only randomised mortality figure is 8%, and the survival benefit of surgery rests on non-randomised comparison.
new.proposal: Offer conversion surgery only after an objective response and only where R0 is achievable, with a second opinion for responders; do not promise an operation at the start of induction; quote CONKO-007's 8% 30-day mortality, one death in twelve, in the consent conversation. Whether the programme offers it at all is left to the group.
new.proposal_locator: Gate 7 · Standard 'Offer conversion surgery only where R0 is achievable, and only after an objective response.' (note); Avoid 'Do not promise an operation at the start of induction therapy.'; Standard 'Re-ask the resectability question…'
new.rationale: CONKO-007 is the only randomised trial that reports it: of 336 patients randomised after three months of induction without progression, 122 (36% to 37%) reached theatre, 73 of 336 (22%) achieved R0, and 30-day postoperative mortality was 8% in both arms (5 of 60 and 5 of 62). The survival advantage of surgery within that trial (HR 0.525, 0.408–0.676) is a non-randomised comparison of operated with non-operated patients. LAP07, from gemcitabine-based induction, reached resection in 18 of 442 patients (4%). The 159 of 495 patients (32.1%) who progressed during induction had a median survival of 9 months with no 5-year survivors. The group must decide whether it offers this at all, to whom, and with what number on the consent form.
new.audit: Registry: proportion reaching exploration and resection, R0 rate with millimetre clearance, 30- and 90-day mortality, and overall survival from the start of induction including patients who progressed before any surgical assessment.

changes.old: Downgraded from A to B on the full-text read. Overall survival was a secondary endpoint that became significant only on the final of several analyses, nine years after the primary report, with no multiplicity adjustment reported for the repeated testing. The authors themselves note that because relapse was common in the first year and gemcitabine was standard therapy at relapse, the design is better read as immediate versus delayed gemcitabine than as chemotherapy versus none. The primary disease-free survival endpoint was assessed in part by abdominal ultrasound every 8 weeks with no central radiology review and recurrence dated from the first subjective symptom, in an open-label trial — which is why a 2.4-fold disease-free survival difference sits beside a 2.6-month median survival difference. Eighteen of 186 patients (10%) never started gemcitabine, mainly for postoperative complications, and only 62% completed all six cycles. Enrolment ran 1998 to 2004 across 88 centres with no central pathology review and no uniform margin definition, so neither its R1 rate nor its 20.2-month observation arm is a usable benchmark today.

The authors themselves note that because relapse was common in the first year and gemcitabine was standard therapy at relapse, the design is better read as immediate versus delayed gemcitabine than as chemotherapy versus none. old.t: Define in advance what counts as growth, record a rate rather than a size, and say plainly that no growth threshold in use has been derived.
old.pref: Two thresholds are in circulation and the board should pick one and write it down. PANDORA used growth of more than 0.5 cm per year as its protocol trigger, and 8 of 76 patients (11%) met it at a median of 17 months. The 2025 MEN1 recommendations use growth of under 1 mm per year as the point at which the imaging interval may be lengthened to every 1 to 2 years, at 92% panel agreement, with intervals individualised to the observed growth rate and the absolute size. In ASPEN, increasing size was the stated indication for surgery in only 4 of the 406 surveillance patients, against patient preference in 42 of 94 operated patients and centre preference in 37.
old.avoid: Do not present either number as biological - neither has any cited derivation. One millimetre a year lies below the measurement reproducibility of serial cross-sectional imaging of a small pancreatic lesion across different scanners and readers, and will generate both false stability and false progression. Half a centimetre a year is no better founded: in PANDORA the 8 patients who met it had a mean size at last follow-up of still only 1.2 cm (SD 0.7), and only 2 of them ever crossed 2.0 cm, so the threshold was detecting measurement variation as much as growth. What makes either threshold usable at all is the same modality, the same contrast agent and the same measurement convention every time, which is the one part of this that is entirely within the programme's control.
old.note: Record the measurement in the body of the note, in millimetres, naming the phase and sequence it was made on. A growth rate that cannot be recomputed from the chart is not a growth rate. See approval 12.

changes.old: Analogues suppress the counter-regulatory hormones — growth hormone, glucagon and catecholamines — and in a receptor-negative insulinoma can precipitously worsen hypoglycaemia with fatal complications reported. About two-thirds of insulinomas are receptor-PET negative, so this is a common trap rather than a rare one, and it is why the receptor scan is obtained before the drug.

old.t: For appropriate sporadic, localized functioning tumours, the hormonal syndrome can justify resection irrespective of size. MEN1-associated gastrinoma requires individualized hereditary and endocrine assessment.
old.pref: Every localised functional tumour without distant metastases, where resection serves both symptom control and cure. Malignant potential runs from 5–15% for insulinoma to 60–90% for gastrinoma, glucagonoma and tumours secreting VIP, PTHrP or ectopic ACTH, so for everything except insulinoma the operation is an oncologic one. Resection of a localised insulinoma gives a 98% biochemical cure rate with a 6% chance of recurrence at 10 years.
old.avoid: Do not apply the small-nonfunctional observation rule to a functional tumour. NCCN's resection requirement for glucagonoma, VIPoma and somatostatinoma is total removal with negative margins, including adjacent organs where involved, with regional nodes — pancreatoduodenectomy for the head, distal pancreatectomy with or without splenectomy for body and tail.
old.note: Biochemical cure for apparently sporadic gastrinoma is 60% immediately after resection and 30-40% at 5 years, with 15-year disease-free survival of 15%, so "cured" means something different in each syndrome and should be said in those terms. changes.source_locator: Full_Text_Review_2026-10-31/Analyst_A_Full_Reaudit_2026-11-01/reviews/pancreatic_ampullary/Source_Reviews/31856076_NANETS_surgical.md; 26482044_Tang.md; original ENETS NEC guidance PMID36924180 PDF pp5–8 (shared source application)
changes.old: NANETS states that patients with poorly differentiated carcinoma, small or large cell, should not undergo resection, given the aggressive behaviour and extremely poor prognosis that does not appear to be affected by surgery. ENETS 2023 allows that surgery can benefit localised disease after extensive preoperative imaging, and places carboplatin with etoposide first line in metastatic disease, with irinotecan and a fluoropyrimidine as the best-evidenced second line; median survival in metastatic disease is 11 to 12 months.
changes.new: NANETS 2020 generally advises against resection of pancreatic NEC. ENETS 2023 permits selected localized disease to be considered for surgery after thorough staging, with perioperative treatment discussed. Differentiation informs care but is not the sole determinant: integrate stage, anatomy, fitness and expected benefit. Metastatic NEC generally follows a systemic-therapy pathway.

changes.old: Grade D, and the borrowed schedule is now known to disagree with its own source. The published follow-up recommendations for completely resected gastroenteropancreatic tumours - a 22-member RAND/UCLA panel scoring 193 scenarios against an evidence base of 6 eligible studies plus two then-unpublished cohorts - recommend for a resected pancreatic tumour consultation with triple-phase CT or MRI yearly for 3 years, then every 1 to 2 years to a total of 10 years, deliberately de-intensifying the first three years relative to NCCN, ENETS, ESMO and NANETS while extending surveillance past ten. They also recommend no follow-up at all for a grade 1, node-negative pancreatic tumour smaller than 2 cm. That exemption is expert opinion at a 75% agreement threshold, in a dataset whose cumulative recurrence was 33.5% at 5 years and 48.5% at 10 and whose median time to pancreatic recurrence was 7.2 years, and node-negative in a small tumour usually means few or no nodes were taken. It applies to resected patients and not to observed ones, and this page does not adopt it - but the group should know that the schedule it borrows is contradicted by the paper it is borrowed from. ENETS 2023 sets a third schedule again, imaging at 3 to 6 months after curative resection, then every 6 to 12 months for 5 years, every 12 to 24 months to 10 years and then every 5 years, at level 5 evidence graded B, with patients told to expect at least 20 years and possibly lifelong surveillance. See approval 13.

changes.old: This schedule is consensus, not trial-derived, and the three consensus sources disagree with one another. NCCN starts at 12 weeks to 12 months and runs to a maximum of 10 years. ENETS 2023 starts at 3 to 6 months with a somatostatin-receptor PET, then every 6 to 12 months for 5 years, every 12 to 24 months to 10 years and then every 5 years, at level 5 evidence graded B - an inversion the GRADE framework it claims to follow would not permit. The RAND/UCLA follow-up recommendations for completely resected gastroenteropancreatic tumours deliberately de-intensify the first three years - yearly imaging for 3 years, then every 1 to 2 years to 10, with the decision to continue or stop discussed with the patient at 10 - while extending beyond 10, and exempt a grade 1, node-negative pancreatic tumour under 2 cm from follow-up altogether. That exemption came from a 22-member panel at a 75% agreement threshold, over an evidence base of 6 eligible studies plus two then-unpublished cohorts that carried no grade, stage or margin data - the very variables the recommendations stratify on. See approval 13.

changes.old: Characterise with MRI, including diffusion-weighted imaging, rather than repeating the CT — but order it for the sub-centimetre lesion, which is the only place MRI has been shown to beat CT.
changes.new: Characterize an indeterminate liver lesion in a patient with known extrahepatic cancer using a test chosen for the lesion size, initial modality and clinical question; contrast MRI is often appropriate.

changes.source_locator: Full_Text_Review_2026-10-31/Analyst_A_Full_Reaudit_2026-11-01/reviews/metastatic_benign/Source_Reviews/20829538.md; Niekel 2010 PDF p4
changes.old: Do not overstate the margin. In a meta-analysis of 39 prospective studies and 3,391 untreated colorectal cancer patients, per-lesion sensitivity was 80.3% (95% CI 74.6-85.0) for MRI against 74.4% (68.7-79.3) for CT — overlapping intervals, no significant difference — and per-patient sensitivity 88.2% (64.8-96.8) against 83.6% (66.9-92.8), p=0.653, also not significant. The one real advantage is below 10 mm: 60.2% (54.4-65.7) for MRI against 47.3% (40.1-54.5) for CT, p=0.006. At 10 mm or larger there is no difference at all, 89.0% against 86.7%, p=0.617. Note also what the meta-analysis did not find: liver-specific contrast material, multisection scanners and dual-phase acquisition each gave no measurable benefit, so the case for MRI rests on the sequences and not on the agent.
changes.new: The 2010 meta-analysis concerns untreated colorectal-cancer staging. Its subcentimetre advantage for MRI does not restrict MRI to small lesions, and a nonsignificant comparison at ≥10 mm does not prove equivalence. Gadoxetate and gadobenate were not represented sufficiently to support a claim that modern liver-specific contrast agents provide no benefit.

changes.source_locator: Full_Text_Review_2026-10-31/Analyst_A_Full_Reaudit_2026-11-01/reviews/metastatic_benign/Source_Reviews/28927870.md; Gore 2017 Figure 1 and PDF pp6–7; 33153555 ACR variant tables
changes.old: Any indeterminate lesion in a patient with a known extrahepatic malignancy. The ACR incidental-findings algorithm names MRI as the modality for further workup in all four of its core recommendations, and the ACR Appropriateness Criteria make MRI without and with intravenous contrast the only option rated usually appropriate for a sub-centimetre lesion found on ultrasound in a patient with a known extrahepatic malignancy.
changes.new: Use the scenario-specific ACR guidance. For a lesion <1 cm first seen on ultrasound in a patient with known cancer, contrast MRI is the only test rated usually appropriate in that variant. For a lesion first seen on limited CT or MRI, contrast MRI and multiphase CT may both be appropriate; the initial test and clinical context matter.

changes.old: Ordered by how often each is the right answer in an unselected incidental population, not by any comparative trial — none compares them for this indication. Both are second tests ordered for a named reason; neither characterises a lesion the liver MRI left indeterminate.
changes.new: These are selected second tests. PET/CT may help in an appropriate oncology scenario, and biopsy may resolve a management-changing diagnosis after imaging review. Neither replaces scenario-specific cross-sectional characterization.

changes.source_locator: Full_Text_Review_2026-10-31/Analyst_A_Full_Reaudit_2026-11-01/reviews/metastatic_benign/Source_Reviews/28927870.md; Gore 2017 Figure 1 and PDF pp6–7; 33153555 ACR variant tables
changes.old: This is the ACR algorithm's most consequential single rule and it follows the risk fork at clinical decision 0, not the lesion. In a low-risk patient, lesions 1 cm or smaller require no workup at all. In a high-risk patient, MRI is advised in 3 to 6 months to characterise the lesion and assess growth, and for a sub-centimetre lesion found on ultrasound in a patient with a known extrahepatic malignancy the ACR Appropriateness Criteria make MRI without and with contrast the only option they rate usually appropriate.
changes.new: Apply the ACR CT-incidental algorithm to its intended population. A low-risk lesion <1 cm generally needs no further workup, but suspicious features may justify MRI. A high-risk lesion <1 cm generally receives MRI in 3–6 months, with surveillance CT an alternative in the appropriate oncology setting. Exactly 1.0 cm enters the 1.0–1.5 cm branch. The separate ACR Appropriateness Criteria also depend on how the lesion was first detected.

changes.old: The 8 mm or 15 mm nodule found on a surveillance or incidental study in a cirrhotic liver. Under CT/MRI LI-RADS v2018 the no-arterial-hyperenhancement observations fall into LR-2 or LR-3 depending on size and feature count, and the management LI-RADS specifies is repeat or alternative diagnostic imaging in 3 to 6 months for LR-3, not discharge and not biopsy.
changes.new: Classic benign findings can be LR-1 or LR-2. Other observations without arterial hyperenhancement may be LR-3 or LR-4, depending on size and the remaining features. LR-3 generally receives repeat or alternative diagnostic imaging in 3–6 months; LR-4 warrants multidisciplinary diagnostic planning, which may include biopsy.

changes.source_locator: Full_Text_Review_2026-10-31/Analyst_A_Full_Reaudit_2026-11-01/reviews/metastatic_benign/Source_Reviews/30251931.md; Chernyak 2018 PDF pp6–7 and 10–13; LI-RADS core category tables
changes.old: A targetoid or LR-M observation is a non-HCC malignancy until proved otherwise — route it to the iCCA pathway, and to the cHCC-CCA pathway where both phenotypes are present or the diagnosis is genuinely mixed.
changes.new: An LR-M observation is probably or definitely malignant but is not specific for HCC. Clarify the diagnosis before choosing the HCC, iCCA, mixed-tumour or metastatic treatment pathway.

changes.source_locator: Full_Text_Review_2026-10-31/Analyst_A_Full_Reaudit_2026-11-01/reviews/metastatic_benign/Source_Reviews/30251931.md; Chernyak 2018 PDF pp6–7 and 10–13; LI-RADS core category tables
changes.old: Rim arterial hyperenhancement, peripheral washout, delayed central enhancement, an infiltrative pattern, marked diffusion restriction, or necrosis. 93% (95% CI 87-97) of pooled CT/MRI LR-M observations were malignant but only 36% (26-48) were HCC, which is precisely why the category exists and why it routes away from the HCC page.
changes.new: The differential includes iCCA, combined HCC–CCA and atypical HCC. Historical pooled CT/MRI categories reported 93% malignancy and 36% HCC in LR-M; these are selected, earlier-version cohorts rather than a histologic diagnosis for the individual patient. Discuss tissue sampling and the safest route in the multidisciplinary team.

changes.source_locator: Full_Text_Review_2026-10-31/Analyst_A_Full_Reaudit_2026-11-01/reviews/metastatic_benign/Source_Reviews/30251931.md; Chernyak 2018 PDF pp6–7 and 10–13; LI-RADS core category tables
changes.old: A lesion with both hepatocellular and cholangiocytic phenotypes, or an LR-M observation, goes to clinical decision 8 and to the cHCC-CCA pathway, not into an interval. Downgraded from B to C: the LI-RADS management figures are retrospective and the CEUS evidence is a sub-analysis of a trial powered for a different question.
changes.new: An LR-M or mixed-phenotype observation needs diagnostic clarification at decision 8, often including tissue, rather than routine interval follow-up alone. HCC remains in the differential; route to a disease-specific treatment pathway after clarification.

changes.source_locator: Full_Text_Review_2026-10-31/Analyst_A_Full_Reaudit_2026-11-01/reviews/metastatic_benign/Source_Reviews/30251931.md; Chernyak 2018 PDF pp6–7 and 10–13; LI-RADS core category tables
changes.old: Do not default to the HCC pathway because it is the busiest one. An LR-M observation treated as HCC is the error this assessment exists to prevent, and the pooled CT/MRI LR-M HCC proportion is 36% (95% CI 26-48) — so most LR-M observations are malignancies that are not HCC, and the category routes accordingly.
changes.new: Do not assign an LR-M observation to HCC or cholangiocarcinoma treatment from the category alone. Establish the likely histology and extent through multidisciplinary review and appropriate sampling.

changes.source_locator: Full_Text_Review_2026-10-31/Analyst_A_Full_Reaudit_2026-11-01/reviews/metastatic_benign/Source_Reviews/30251931.md; Chernyak 2018 PDF pp6–7 and 10–13; LI-RADS core category tables
changes.old: Route by primary where there is one: a confirmed colorectal primary is the CRLM pathway, a confirmed neuroendocrine primary is the NELM pathway, and a hepatocellular lesion in a normal liver that is not focal nodular hyperplasia is the HCA pathway.
changes.new: Route confirmed colorectal liver metastases to CRLM and confirmed neuroendocrine liver disease to NELM. A hepatocellular lesion in a normal liver requires positive assessment for HCA and exclusion of HCC; exclusion of FNH alone does not diagnose HCA.

changes.source_locator: Full_Text_Review_2026-10-31/Analyst_A_Full_Reaudit_2026-11-01/reviews/metastatic_benign/Priority_Clinical_Corrections.md; local CPG applies transplant-selection requirements separately
changes.old: Do not route on a presumption. The local CPG requires colorectal origin to be confirmed and the primary's resection and the absence of active extrahepatic disease to be verified before the CRLM destination, and requires central pathology review of grade and differentiation before the neuroendocrine one.
changes.new: Early cancer-roadmap referral does not require the colorectal primary already resected or extrahepatic disease absent; those factors affect treatment and transplant assessment later. Confirm the likely origin, and obtain expert pathology review of neuroendocrine grade and differentiation when relevant.

changes.source_locator: Full_Text_Review_2026-10-31/Analyst_A_Full_Reaudit_2026-11-01/reviews/metastatic_benign/Source_Reviews/38958301.md; ACG 2024 original PDF pp13–16; EASL 2016 HCA recommendations
changes.old: Do not let a reassuring subtype override size, growth, male sex or an exophytic position, and do not let an unreassuring subtype alone commit a patient to an operation that size and growth do not justify. EASL states that whether the haemorrhage or malignant-transformation risk attributed to beta-catenin activation is independent of sex, size and rate of change is presently unknown, and that prospective validation of imaging-based subtyping is necessary before widespread implementation. The 0 of 47 figure is also a resection-series denominator and is small: it excludes nothing above a few per cent.
changes.new: Do not let a reassuring imaging phenotype cancel risk from sex, size, growth or bleeding. Imaging subtype alone is not equivalent to a confirmed molecular diagnosis. Proven beta-catenin activation, particularly a high-risk exon 3 alteration, warrants specialist assessment for resection irrespective of size under EASL/ACG guidance; document the exon/codon and diagnostic certainty.

changes.source_locator: Full_Text_Review_2026-10-31/Analyst_A_Full_Reaudit_2026-11-01/reviews/metastatic_benign/Source_Reviews/38958301.md; ACG 2024 original PDF pp13–16; EASL 2016 HCA recommendations
changes.old: Reimage with contrast-enhanced MRI at 6 months, and treat that scan as a trajectory rather than a verdict — six months is too early to call risk-factor modification a failure.
changes.new: Reimage after risk-factor modification and assess the trajectory. In women with lesions ≥5 cm, individualize reassessment and intervention over 6–12 months unless bleeding, concerning growth or suspected malignancy requires earlier action.

changes.source_locator: Full_Text_Review_2026-10-31/Analyst_A_Full_Reaudit_2026-11-01/reviews/metastatic_benign/Source_Reviews/38958301.md; ACG 2024 original PDF pp13–16; EASL 2016 HCA recommendations
changes.old: Every presumed adenoma. EASL advises reassessment with contrast-enhanced MRI after 6 months for all presumed adenomas, and in women a period of 6 months observation after lifestyle change (evidence level II-3, grade of recommendation 2). ACG 2024 uses a looser 6- to 12-month interval and does not tie it to a size trigger (conditional recommendation, low quality of evidence). The Italian multisociety guideline specifies MRI at 6 months after contraceptive discontinuation, repeat at 1 year if unchanged or reduced below 5 cm, and annual ultrasound after the first 18 months — and grades every one of those steps very low quality (D), conditional.
changes.new: EASL recommends six months of observation after lifestyle change in women, then resection for lesions ≥5 cm or continuing to grow. ACG 2024 allows 6–12 months for an appropriate woman with a lesion ≥5 cm before deciding on treatment; this timing and size statement is an ungraded key concept. Individualize continued observation of a shrinking, otherwise low-risk lesion.

changes.source_locator: Full_Text_Review_2026-10-31/Analyst_A_Full_Reaudit_2026-11-01/reviews/metastatic_benign/Source_Reviews/38958301.md; ACG 2024 original PDF pp13–16; EASL 2016 HCA recommendations
changes.old: Adenoma still larger than 5 cm after an adequate trial of risk-factor modification — and an explicit note of how long that trial has run, because six months is too early
changes.new: Adenoma persistently ≥5 cm after an individualized trial of risk-factor modification, with duration, regression trajectory and any high-risk exception recorded

changes.source_locator: Full_Text_Review_2026-10-31/Analyst_A_Full_Reaudit_2026-11-01/reviews/metastatic_benign/Source_Reviews/38958301.md; ACG 2024 original PDF pp13–16; EASL 2016 HCA recommendations
changes.old: Treat a lesion that is persistently larger than 5 cm, or growing by 20% or more, as an indication for curative treatment — and say plainly, to the patient and in the note, that 5 cm is a convention and not a derived threshold.
changes.new: Assess resection for a persistently ≥5 cm or growing adenoma after appropriate risk-factor modification; account for subtype, sex, symptoms, bleeding and suspicion of malignancy.

changes.source_locator: Full_Text_Review_2026-10-31/Analyst_A_Full_Reaudit_2026-11-01/reviews/metastatic_benign/Source_Reviews/38958301.md; ACG 2024 original PDF pp13–16; EASL 2016 HCA recommendations
changes.old: At least 6 months of adequate risk-factor modification documented for non-urgent oestrogen- or weight-associated disease
changes.new: For non-urgent oestrogen- or weight-associated disease, document the adequate modification period and trajectory; six months alone does not establish failure, particularly while a lesion is regressing

changes.source_locator: Full_Text_Review_2026-10-31/Analyst_A_Full_Reaudit_2026-11-01/reviews/metastatic_benign/Source_Reviews/38958301.md; ACG 2024 original PDF pp13–16; EASL 2016 HCA recommendations
changes.old: Unresectable liver adenomatosis with more than 10 adenomas AND at least one of: recurrent or life-threatening haemorrhage or prior rupture not controllable by embolisation or targeted resection; confirmed or strongly suspected malignant transformation, or a high-risk molecular subtype; a syndromic driver or underlying liver disease independently threatening hepatic function; or documented progression despite at least 6 months of adequate risk-factor modification with liver-directed options exhausted or contraindicated.
changes.new: Unresectable liver adenomatosis with more than 10 adenomas AND at least one of: recurrent or life-threatening haemorrhage or prior rupture not controllable by embolisation or targeted resection; confirmed or strongly suspected malignant transformation, or a high-risk molecular subtype; a syndromic driver or underlying liver disease independently threatening hepatic function; or documented progression despite an adequate, individualized risk-factor-modification period, with the trajectory and reason for intervention recorded with liver-directed options exhausted or contraindicated.

changes.source_locator: Full_Text_Review_2026-10-31/Analyst_A_Full_Reaudit_2026-11-01/reviews/metastatic_benign/Source_Reviews/31313827.md; van Rosmalen 2019 original PDF pp3–8, Table 2/Figure 2; Supplement Table S1
changes.old: Do not invoke it before embolisation and ablation have been assessed by the services that perform them, with the assessment in writing. Elective embolisation avoided surgery in 41 of 49 patients (84%) in one systematic review and reduced median diameter from 76 to 48 mm in a 59-patient multicentre series, so exhausted has to mean assessed and rejected, not untried — but present the other half too, because the patient will ask: 34% of embolised patients still needed surgery, 10% had a grade D complication, one died at three months, and symptoms were unchanged.
changes.new: Do not invoke it before embolisation and ablation have been assessed by the services that perform them, with the assessment in writing. Elective embolisation avoided surgery in 41 of 49 patients (84%) in one systematic review and reduced median diameter from 76 to 48 mm in a 59-patient multicentre series, so exhausted has to mean assessed and rejected, not untried — but present the other half too, because the patient will ask: 34% of embolised patients still needed surgery, 10% had a grade D complication, one died at three months, and symptoms decreased from 34/59 (58%) to 22/59 (37%), without a statistically significant difference (P=.134); long-term benefit remains uncertain.

changes.source_locator: Full_Text_Review_2026-10-31/Analyst_A_Full_Reaudit_2026-11-01/reviews/metastatic_benign/Source_Reviews/31313827.md; van Rosmalen 2019 original PDF pp3–8, Table 2/Figure 2; Supplement Table S1
changes.old: Two local approval items. First: will the programme accept elective embolisation as a first-line alternative to resection in a good surgical candidate who prefers it? EASL reserves embolisation for poor surgical candidates. The 84% elective surgery-avoidance figure rests on 49 patients from multiple small series with no common protocol, and against it sit 10% grade D complications, one reported death three months after the procedure, 34% of patients still requiring surgery, unchanged symptoms at 3 months, no histology, and a pooled follow-up too short to detect transformation — a decision requiring explicit discussion of benefits and risks. Second: does the programme adopt a composite trigger — 5 cm, or growth of 20%, or exophytic position, or visible lesional arteries, or a segment II-III location — in place of diameter alone? Correction: the earlier draft asserted that the position and vascularity effects came out larger than diameter in one cohort. Those effect sizes could not be confirmed in the full-text read and have been withdrawn, so this item cannot be decided until someone reads that paper's positional analysis directly; what the paper does establish is a fitted cut-point at 35 mm. Registry: modality chosen, diameter change, complication by Clavien-Dindo grade, subsequent intervention, specimen or explant finding.

changes.source_locator: Full_Text_Review_2026-10-31/Analyst_A_Full_Reaudit_2026-11-01/reviews/metastatic_benign/Source_Reviews/31313827.md; van Rosmalen 2019 original PDF pp3–8, Table 2/Figure 2; Supplement Table S1
changes.old: EASL reserves embolisation for poor surgical candidates. The data since show 84% surgery avoidance after elective embolisation, on 49 patients from multiple small series, and a fall in median diameter from 76 to 48 mm. Against that: 10% grade D complications, one reported death three months after the procedure, 34% of patients still requiring surgery, no symptom improvement at 3 months (P=0.134), viable tissue and no histology left behind in a disease where 20-40% of presumed adenomas prove to be something else, and a pooled follow-up of 31 months too short to detect transformation. That is a shared decision the programme should endorse or decline explicitly, with the harms disclosed, rather than leave to individual preference.

changes.source_locator: Full_Text_Review_2026-10-31/Analyst_A_Full_Reaudit_2026-11-01/reviews/metastatic_benign/Source_Reviews/35018302.md; Ziogas 2022 Tables 1–4 and cause-of-death results
changes.old: Ordered as the local protocol lists them, not by outcome — no comparison of routes exists, and the whole indication rests on 142 US transplants across 33 years and 49 European ones across 27. Published survival is good: patient survival 94.2%, 89.7% and 86.3% at 1, 3 and 5 years over a median 62.9 months in the UNOS cohort of 142, with graft survival 89.3%, 84.1% and 80.0%, and 95% at all three points across 99 published cases. Read those as what a heavily selected cohort achieves rather than as a treatment effect, and read the other side of them: crude waitlist mortality was 9.0% among the 199 listed, death occurred in 26 of 142 (18.3%) during follow-up, 24 of the 142 transplants were for adenoma diagnosed only incidentally on the explant, 89.4% had no carcinoma at all, and the median laboratory MELD at transplant was 8 at a median age of 34.5 — young people with preserved liver function, so almost all of that mortality is attributable to the treatment rather than the disease. The registry records neither the number nor the size of the adenomas, and the 99 published cases report 6.0% mortality against the registry's 18.3%, a threefold disagreement the authors attribute to publication bias in their own review.
