changes.source_locator: Full_Text_Review_2026-10-31/Analyst_A_Full_Reaudit_2026-11-01/reviews/metastatic_benign/Source_Reviews/35018302.md; Ziogas 2022 Tables 1–4 and cause-of-death results
changes.old: Grade D, and the governance question behind approval item 10. In UNOS from 1987 to 2020, 199 patients were listed with crude waitlist mortality of 18 of 199 (9.0%) and 142 were transplanted at a median age of 34.5 with a median laboratory MELD of 8 — young people with preserved liver function — of whom 127 (89.4%) had no carcinoma; death occurred in 26 of 142 (18.3%) over a median 62.9 months, with 5-year patient survival 86.3% and graft survival 80.0%. Because the recipients were not in liver failure, almost all of that mortality is attributable to the treatment rather than the disease. 61.3% received MELD exception points although only 6.3% had glycogen storage disease and 4.9% a listing carcinoma codiagnosis, so the exception pathway functions as a discretionary route rather than a rule. And the registry records neither the number nor the size of the adenomas, so the largest experience of the most radical treatment in this disease contains no data on the variable the rest of the pathway turns on. The European adenomatosis registry found true malignant transformation in only 17 of 49 explants (35%) with three operative deaths, five retransplantations and three fatal carcinoma recurrences — roughly one patient in eight dying of the treatment or its failure, against a 2.5% ten-year transformation rate in adenomatosis managed conservatively — and 15 of 64 registry-coded cases proved not to be adenomatosis at all on verification. The accompanying systematic review of 99 published cases reports 6.0% mortality against UNOS's 18.3%, a threefold disagreement its own authors attribute to publication bias in their review. Neither dataset has a comparison group managed without transplantation, so the claim of excellent outcomes in well-selected patients is unfalsifiable from these data. The 2025 UK national guidance assigns patients to four eligibility categories by consensus with no cohort behind them and no reference to beta-catenin or sonic hedgehog status.

changes.source_locator: Full_Text_Review_2026-10-31/Analyst_A_Full_Reaudit_2026-11-01/reviews/metastatic_benign/Source_Reviews/26919265.md; Chiche 2016 original Figure 1, Tables 3–4 and Results
changes.old: Lesion number alone does not qualify. The European registry experience is the cautionary case: of 49 transplants performed for adenomatosis, true malignant transformation was present in only 17 explants (35%), there were three operative deaths and five retransplantations, and three patients developed carcinoma recurrence, all fatal — so roughly one patient in eight died of the treatment or its failure, against a 2.5% ten-year transformation rate in adenomatosis managed conservatively. The same series found that 15 of 64 cases coded as adenomatosis in the registry were not adenomatosis at all once verified, which is a warning about every registry-based figure in this disease.
changes.new: Lesion number alone does not qualify. The European registry experience is the cautionary case: of 49 transplants performed for adenomatosis, 17 patients had HCC before or at transplantation; the detailed tables record 12 positive explants, four negative explants after prior HCC and one unavailable result, there were three operative deaths and five retransplantations, and three patients developed carcinoma recurrence, all fatal — so roughly one patient in eight died of the treatment or its failure, against a 2.5% ten-year transformation rate in adenomatosis managed conservatively. The same series found that 15 of 64 cases coded as adenomatosis in the registry were not adenomatosis at all once verified, which is a warning about every registry-based figure in this disease.

changes.old: Three local approval items. First: does the programme open an adenoma transplant route at all, and under whose governance? The indication is rare enough that most centres will see one candidate in several years, graft stewardship for a benign disease is an institutional judgement, and neither supporting dataset has a comparison group managed without transplantation — so the claim of excellent outcomes in well-selected patients is unfalsifiable from these data. Second: does the S45 and exon 7/8 restriction stand as written, given that the genotype-phenotype data make S45 a special case — a weak activator in benign tumours that is duplicated to high activity in most carcinomas, with chromosome 3p gain or copy-neutral loss of heterozygosity in 37% of weakly mutated carcinomas against none of 34 adenomas — rather than a low-risk one? Third: who verifies the live OPTN Policy 9.4 and 9.5 text and the current transplant-oncology guidance before each submission, and on what cycle? Several items in the protocol are marked VERIFY and remain unverified. One further caution from the full-text read: 15 of 64 cases coded as adenomatosis in the European registry were not adenomatosis once verified, and the US analysis rests on the same kind of coding plus a free-text search with no case-level verification, so every registry figure behind this assessment should be read as provisional. Registry: route named, full lesion dataset, CTNNB1 result and method, review-board decision, waitlist events, donor source, explant pathology concordance with the preoperative diagnosis, perioperative morbidity and mortality, graft and patient survival, and malignant transformation.

changes.old: Two series and a review, all retrospective and all heavily selected. UNOS 1987-2020: 199 patients listed with crude waitlist mortality of 18 of 199 (9.0%); 142 transplanted at a median age 34.5, 79.6% female, 22.5% children, median laboratory MELD at transplant 8 — these were not patients with failing livers; 127 of 142 (89.4%) had no carcinoma; death in 26 of 142 (18.3%) over a median 62.9 months, with patient survival 94.2%, 89.7% and 86.3% at 1, 3 and 5 years and graft survival 89.3%, 84.1% and 80.0%. Because the recipients were young with preserved liver function, almost all of that mortality is attributable to the treatment rather than to the disease. 61.3% received MELD exception points although only 6.3% had glycogen storage disease and 4.9% a listing carcinoma codiagnosis. The registry records neither the number nor the size of the adenomas, so the largest experience of the most radical treatment in this disease contains no data on the variable the rest of the pathway turns on. European registry, adenomatosis: 49 transplants with true malignant transformation in 17 explants (35%), three operative deaths, five retransplantations and three fatal carcinoma recurrences — roughly one patient in eight died of the treatment or its failure, against a 2.5% ten-year transformation rate in adenomatosis managed conservatively; and 15 of 64 registry-coded cases were not adenomatosis at all once verified. The accompanying systematic review of 99 published cases reports 6.0% mortality against 18.3% in UNOS, a threefold disagreement the authors attribute to publication bias in their own review

changes.old: Name the source of each extrapolation when consenting, and say that the two trials doing most of the work excluded this disease by design. Capecitabine–gemcitabine rests on ESPAC-4, a trial of resected pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma in which nonductal pancreatic tumours were an explicit exclusion criterion: 730 patients analysed, median overall survival 28.0 months (95% CI 23.5–31.5) against 25.5 (22.7–27.9), hazard ratio 0.82 (0.68–0.98), P=0.032 — a 2.5-month median gain whose upper confidence limit almost touches 1, reported early on a monitoring committee's recommendation at 458 of a planned 480 deaths with no alpha adjustment presented, with the benefit concentrated in R0 patients (39.5 against 27.9 months) and essentially no separation in R1 disease (23.7 against 23.0 months), and grade 3–4 adverse events in 226 of 359 patients (63%) against 196 of 366 (54%). Modified FOLFIRINOX rests on PRODIGE-24, also resected pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma with nonductal tumours excluded, and with entry restricted to WHO performance status 0–1, age under 80 and CA 19-9 under 180 U/mL: 493 patients, median disease-free survival 21.6 months (17.7–27.6) against 12.8 (11.7–15.2), hazard ratio 0.58 (0.46–0.73), P<0.001, median overall survival 54.4 against 35.0 months, hazard ratio 0.64 (0.48–0.86), P=0.003, at the cost of grade 3–4 toxicity in 180 of 237 patients (75.9%) against 128 of 242 (52.9%), and with an imprecise disease-free survival estimate in the 101 patients aged 70 or over (HR 0.86, 0.53–1.39), which does not establish absence of benefit. Capecitabine rests on BILCAP in biliary tract cancer, whose own primary analysis was not significant (median overall survival 51.1 against 36.4 months, P=0.097), and on X-ACT in colon cancer for the intestinal subtype; cisplatin–gemcitabine on ABC-02 in advanced biliary tract cancer, which did include ampullary cancers but did not report how many and was not an adjuvant trial (11.7 against 8.1 months, hazard ratio 0.64, 0.52–0.80, P<0.001); and CapeOx on a 31-patient phase II trial in advanced small bowel and ampullary cancers of which 12 were ampullary, again not adjuvant. BILCAP and ABC-02 are cited here from their abstracts and from guideline text only, since neither full text was read for this page.

changes.old: Do not treat any of these backbones as validated in this disease. ABC-02 randomised 410 patients with locally advanced or metastatic cholangiocarcinoma, gallbladder cancer or ampullary cancer to cisplatin–gemcitabine or gemcitabine, giving median overall survival 11.7 against 8.1 months (hazard ratio 0.64, 95% CI 0.52–0.80, P<0.001) and progression-free survival 8.0 against 5.0 months (P<0.001) — but the number of ampullary patients was not reported, so the ampullary effect size is unknown; that trial is cited here from its abstract and from guideline text only. NCCN states that data for systemic therapy in ampullary cancer are very limited and that the recommendations are extrapolated from pancreatic, colorectal and biliary tract cancer.

changes.old: Intestinal-type regimens follow the colorectal pattern and pancreatobiliary regimens the pancreatic and biliary pattern — which is a reasonable inference from the genomic concordance, and still an inference built on a morphological call with an interobserver κ of 0.39. Graded D rather than C because not one of the regimens on these lists has been tested in a trial that reports an ampullary population: the nearest, ABC-02, included ampullary patients without counting them, and the rest excluded nonductal tumours outright. Clinical trial entry should be screened at the same visit, and in this setting that is the strongest single recommendation on the assessment. [PROTOCOL]
changes.new: Subtype-directed selection partly extrapolates from colorectal, pancreatic and biliary cancers. ABC-02 did include 20 ampullary patients, with an imprecise subgroup OS HR of 0.62 (95% CI 0.21–1.82). ABC-06 separately included 11 ampullary patients after GemCis progression; it informs the subsequent-treatment discussion below, not first-line or adjuvant therapy. Screen for clinical trials and explain these population limits. [PROTOCOL]

changes.old: This is a second draft, revised on 7 October 2026 after a full-text read of the paper depot behind it. There is still no ratified Memorial Hermann roadmap for ampullary tumours, no alignment worksheet behind it, and no institutional position has been taken on any of the fifteen items in the approvals list — the page is a proposal for a multidisciplinary group to argue with, not a statement of practice. What the full-text read changed. Twenty-eight of the thirty-five cited papers were read in full and abstracted with their authors' stated limitations and an independent critique, and the revision moved the page in three material ways. First, ESPAC-3 can no longer be cited as establishing adjuvant benefit in ampullary cancer: the trial was never powered for its ampullary subgroup, reports no hypothesis test for ampullary-only survival anywhere, and the ampullary medians of 40.6, 57.8 and 70.8 months appear without a P value; its primary analysis was negative (hazard ratio 0.86, 95% CI 0.66–1.11, P=0.25), its adjusted analysis (0.75, 0.57–0.98, P=0.03) adjusted for four variables on two of which the observation arm was prognostically worse at baseline, and in its 96 intrapancreatic bile duct patients chemotherapy was numerically worse than observation. Adjuvant chemotherapy remains on the page and is now graded C and offered as a reasonable choice rather than a demonstrated benefit. Second, the subtype question has been rewritten as an asymmetric dispute rather than a tie: the reproducibility study is the ceiling on all of it (κ 0.39, all five observers agreeing in 23% of 232 cases, 40% of tumours mixed, pure intestinal only 6%, survival differing only after the mixed cases were force-assigned, and the subtype failing multivariable analysis at P=0.39), and of the two adjuvant cohorts the positive one allocated treatment at tumour board by prognosis with no adjustment of any kind and reports a whole-cohort result running the other way (hazard ratio 1.124, P=0.608) while the negative one propensity-matched on the actual selection drivers and handled immortal time bias — so the divergence is explained by cohort and method rather than by chance, although the negative result is still underpowered to exclude a modest benefit. Third, the European comparison of papillectomy with surgical ampullectomy is now read for its indication finding first: final histology was neither adenoma nor adenocarcinoma in 24.2% of papillectomies and 14.8% of surgical ampullectomies while advanced disease was found in 10.9% and 36.6%, so roughly a third of the procedures in both arms were done for the wrong indication; papillectomy R0 for adenoma falls from 80.2% to 65.9% once index-session ablation is counted as a probable R2 resection; and papillectomy failed in roughly two-thirds of T1 cancers. Borrowed evidence. ESPAC-4 and PRODIGE-24 are trials of resected pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma that excluded nonductal tumours by design and report no ampullary patients; the page now says so wherever it uses them, as it does for the preoperative biliary drainage trial (cancer of the pancreatic head, plastic stents, no ampullary subgroup), BILCAP (biliary tract), ABC-02 (advanced biliary tract, ampullary patients included but not counted), X-ACT (colon) and the randomised evidence against extended lymphadenectomy (pancreatic). Cited from abstract only. Five papers were sought and not obtained for this revision. Three of them — the 91-patient malignancy prediction cohort (23442830), the EUS preoperative evaluation series (30834717) and the 14-patient ampullary neuroendocrine tumour series (27457864) — have since been read in full; the other two, the National Cancer Database node-yield analysis (PMID 38353072) and the intraductal ultrasound and transpapillary biopsy series (22319960), are still cited from abstract only, and every string that uses them says so. BILCAP (30922733) and ABC-02 (20375404) were also not part of the full-text read and are quoted from their abstracts and from guideline text. Guideline sources, unchanged from the first draft. The programme-supplied machine-converted extraction of the NCCN Ampullary Adenocarcinoma guideline, which carries no version string and which misstates ESPAC-3 on its adjuvant systemic-therapy page while stating it correctly in its discussion (see nonpm, and approvals item 10) — the full-text read confirms that discrepancy from the trial side; the NCCN Pancreatic Adenocarcinoma extraction for the margin, specimen and lymphadenectomy questions the two diseases share; the Brescia PERIPAN international multidisciplinary consensus guidelines of 29 July 2025 for the anatomic definitions, the subtype definitions, the biopsy and specimen-handling recommendations and the reflex mismatch-repair position; the ESGE guideline on endoscopic management of ampullary tumours of 2021 and the ESGE polyposis guideline of 2019 for the endoscopic and familial decision points; and AJCC 8th edition staging as reproduced in NCCN. Every PMID in refs was verified against PubMed on 6 October 2026 to confirm it resolves to the paper cited. Readers should know that nine of eleven main ESGE ampullary recommendations are strong on low-quality evidence, that almost every PERIPAN recommendation is low evidence or expert opinion with its promised AGREE II quality score and audience vote never reported, and that PERIPAN's 30% threshold for the mixed subtype has no stated derivation. Where the sources disagree — on whether subtype should direct adjuvant therapy, on surveillance intervals by Spigelman stage, on whether mismatch-repair and molecular testing is reflex, indication-driven or discouraged, on the minimum node yield, and on what to do with an invasive carcinoma found in a margin-negative papillectomy specimen — the page shows the disagreement and places the choice in a flagnote and in approvals rather than resolving it. Evidence strings carry both halves of every result. Grades fell in eleven places on this revision and rose nowhere, and each downgrade is explained in the note on the string it belongs to; no recommendation was removed, because the roadmap's positions stand and the page's job is to say how well supported they are. Grades are deliberately low across the benign end of the pathway: most of what is done there rests on retrospective series and expert consensus, and grade D is used where that is the truth. This page does not replace clinician judgement, and every numeric criterion must be verified against the current source before use.

old.t: Local therapy to liver or lung metastases, or surgery, in selected oligometastatic patients who have responded to systemic therapy.
old.pref: NCCN lists systemic therapy followed by surgery or other locally directed therapies to liver or lung metastases for select patients with oligometastatic disease and response or stable disease on systemic therapy, after multidisciplinary review.
old.avoid: There is no comparative evidence in ampullary cancer, and the selection that produces the good outcomes is doing the work. Treat it as a protocol and registry activity rather than a standard offer. [REGISTRY] [PROTOCOL]
old.note: The liver is the dominant distant site: 38%–65% of distant recurrences in series reporting site, with peritoneum, lung and bone following. Nodal involvement was the sole predictor of liver metastasis in one analysis.

old.t: Palliative radiotherapy or chemoradiation for symptoms, and palliative care alongside treatment rather than after it.
old.pref: NCCN offers systemic therapy followed by radiotherapy for palliative indications, and palliative radiotherapy for severe pain refractory to analgesic therapy in the subsequent-therapy setting. Palliative and best supportive care run concurrently in every performance-status band, and are the preferred option in ECOG 3.
old.avoid: Do not present palliative radiotherapy as disease control. It is symptom-directed here, and the ampullary-specific evidence is confined to small retrospective series.

new.t: OPEN proposal AMP-R1: local therapy or surgery after systemic response in selected oligometastatic disease; not an activated institutional pathway.
new.pref: NCCN lists systemic therapy followed by surgery or other locally directed therapies to liver or lung metastases for select patients with oligometastatic disease and response or stable disease on systemic therapy, after multidisciplinary review.
new.avoid: There is no comparative evidence in ampullary cancer, and the selection that produces the good outcomes is doing the work. Treat it as a protocol and registry activity rather than a standard offer. [REGISTRY] [PROTOCOL]

Palliative and best supportive care run concurrently in every performance-status band, and are the preferred option in ECOG 3.
new.avoid: Do not present palliative radiotherapy as disease control. It is symptom-directed here, and the ampullary-specific evidence is confined to small retrospective series.

new.t: After progression, reassess fitness, biliary drainage, prior treatment and toxicity, molecular targets and trial options; consider a subsequent regimen when appropriate.
new.pref: For a fit patient after gemcitabine–cisplatin, FOLFOX with active symptom control is a qualified option. ABC-06 enrolled 162 biliary-tract patients with ECOG 0–1 after GemCis progression: median OS 6.2 versus 5.3 months, adjusted HR 0.69 (95% CI 0.50–0.97), against active symptom control alone.
new.avoid: Only 11 patients had ampullary cancer (4 FOLFOX, 7 control); their exploratory OS HR was 0.71 (0.18–2.77). This does not establish an independent ampullary benefit, first-line or adjuvant efficacy, or benefit after prior oxaliplatin. Address drainage, organ function, infection and residual neuropathy before treatment.
new.note: Continue active symptom control throughout. When further anticancer treatment is unsuitable or declined, prioritize supportive care, symptom treatment and goals-of-care planning.

changes.old: The guideline recommends against papillectomy when adenoma has not been proven, but the literature it reviews shows pre-procedure biopsy is wrong in 20-47% of cases in both directions; requiring proof of adenoma from a test that unreliable, while discouraging the biopsy repetition that might establish it, sets a standard that cannot be met in practice
changes.new: ESGE recommends against papillectomy without proven adenoma and explicitly recommends repeat assessment and sampling after initial negative histology when suspicion remains. Figure 1 includes repeated biopsy, EUS-guided sampling and selected limited sphincterotomy pathways. A negative biopsy does not reliably exclude carcinoma.

changes.source_locator: Full_Text_Review_2026-10-31/Analyst_A_Full_Reaudit_2026-11-01/reviews/pancreatic_ampullary/Source_Reviews/PMID_33728632.md; ESGE original PDF pp4–6, Figure1/§3.3; pp8–12 §§4.1,4.3,5; p14 §7
changes.old: The size threshold for en bloc resection is given as '20-30 mm' in the recommendation but discussed elsewhere as 30 mm and as 4 cm for surgical referral, with intraductal involvement thresholds of 10 mm (resectable), 20 mm (surgery suggested) and 20 mm with ablation (possibly acceptable) appearing in different places. The practical cut-points a clinician needs are not stated consistently
changes.new: ESGE separates lesion diameter from ductal extension: en-bloc resection is intended for lesions up to 20–30 mm; 30–40 mm lesions require individualized assessment. Surgery is suggested when endoscopic treatment is technically infeasible, including some lesions >4 cm, or with intraductal extension >20 mm. Expert complementary treatment for lesser ductal extension is a separate context.

changes.source_locator: Full_Text_Review_2026-10-31/Analyst_A_Full_Reaudit_2026-11-01/reviews/pancreatic_ampullary/Source_Reviews/PMID_33728632.md; ESGE original PDF pp4–6, Figure1/§3.3; pp8–12 §§4.1,4.3,5; p14 §7
changes.old: The follow-up schedule - duodenoscopy with scar biopsies at 3, 6 and 12 months then yearly for at least 5 years - is specified to the month on low-quality evidence with no derivation, no interval-cancer analysis and no cost or burden assessment. Subsequent data in this depot show recurrences out to 9.75 years, so 5 years may be too short, while the 3-month examination largely detects residual rather than recurrent disease
changes.new: ESGE specifies surveillance within three months, at six and twelve months, then yearly for at least five years. The minimum is not a fixed stopping point; longer monitoring should reflect recurrence risk, fitness and life expectancy. Evidence for the optimal interval and duration remains limited.

changes.source_locator: Full_Text_Review_2026-10-31/Analyst_A_Full_Reaudit_2026-11-01/reviews/pancreatic_ampullary/Source_Reviews/PMID_33728632.md; ESGE original PDF pp4–6, Figure1/§3.3; pp8–12 §§4.1,4.3,5; p14 §7
changes.old: Do not perform a papillectomy when intraductal extension exceeds 20 mm, when the lesion is over 4 cm, or when a diverticulum prevents access.
changes.new: Refer for surgical or expert endoscopic assessment when papillectomy is technically infeasible, including selected lesions >4 cm or intraductal extension >20 mm.

changes.old: ESGE's own boundary for referring to surgery, with surveillance continuing afterwards either way.
changes.new: ESGE suggests surgical referral on weak, low-quality evidence in these settings. Lesion diameter, intraductal extent and access are distinct considerations; assess 30–40 mm lesions and limited ductal extension individually in an expert centre.

changes.source_locator: Full_Text_Review_2026-10-31/Analyst_A_Full_Reaudit_2026-11-01/reviews/pancreatic_ampullary/Source_Reviews/PMID_33728632.md; ESGE original PDF pp4–6, Figure1/§3.3; pp8–12 §§4.1,4.3,5; p14 §7
changes.old: Do not take on a lesion that cannot be reached or encircled, and do not improvise an en bloc attempt above 30 mm. changes.old: Check availability, regulatory status and coverage before raising it with a patient, and state three limits. The benefit is established only for RAS G12 disease: in patients without a G12 mutation the hazard ratio was 1.38 (95% CI 0.60–3.17), a point estimate favouring chemotherapy. The effect size is inseparable from the comparator's delivery — 38 of 252 patients (15.1%) assigned to chemotherapy never received it against 7 of 248 (2.8%) assigned daraxonrasib, 29 of them withdrawing, and some no longer met eligibility because ECOG had risen above 1 by the time treatment was due, which an oral agent started the same day does not face. And the result is in the previously treated setting only — it says nothing about first line, about the adjuvant setting, or about use around an operation.
changes.new: Benefit was shown in the RAS G12 and overall randomized populations. In the small non-G12 subgroup (n=41), PFS HR was 1.38 (95% CI 0.60–3.17) while OS HR was 0.37 (0.15–0.93); these exploratory, imprecise estimates do not establish lack of benefit. Interpretation also requires the open-label design, short follow-up and differential treatment non-initiation (38/252 chemotherapy versus 7/248 daraxonrasib). Check the current prescribing information and patient-specific toxicity risks.

changes.old: Two operational points matter more than any single row. Order profiling and germline testing at the first visit and bank two extra needle passes at the index biopsy, because the commonest failure in this disease is a report that arrives after the patient is too unwell to act on it — and do not wait for the result to start treatment, since NCCN states that if BRCA1/2 status is unknown the patient is treated as clinically indicated. Then read the denominators. Apart from daraxonrasib and olaparib, every row here is a single-arm result in a pancreatic subset of between one and thirty-eight patients, usually drawn from a mixed-tumour basket trial, with no screening denominator reported, and response rates from baskets do not transfer cleanly to this disease; two of the rows — sotorasib's pancreatic cohort and the subgroup reads from the adagrasib basket — had no prespecified efficacy threshold applying to pancreatic patients at all, so there was nothing they could have failed. Read the germline row the same way: 5.5% is a prevalence estimate from a clinic-based case series compared with public sequencing databases rather than a recruited control group, carriage was not associated with survival, and of the six genes only BRCA1/2 carries a randomised treatment consequence in this disease — so 5.5% is not the actionable fraction. Do not treat the gene as the target; different alterations in the same gene do not predict the same response, which is the point the non-G12 subgroup of RASolute 302 makes (HR 1.38, 0.60–3.17).

opts.name: Daraxonrasib for eligible metastatic PDAC; the US indication is not restricted to a RAS mutation
opts.when: RASolute 302 (phase 3, n=500 randomised, 248 daraxonrasib and 252 investigator's-choice chemotherapy, more than 90% with RAS G12 mutations) had dual primary endpoints in the RAS G12 population and met both: median overall survival 13.2 versus 6.6 months, hazard ratio 0.40, P<0.001, and median progression-free survival by blinded independent central review 7.3 versus 3.5 months, hazard ratio 0.45.
opts.pref: The FDA approval of 26 August 2026 covers adults with metastatic PDAC after at least one systemic therapy, or those not candidates for multiagent systemic therapy. The randomized trial studied patients progressing after one prior line; it does not directly establish the same benefit in untreated patients unfit for combinations.
opts.avoid: Benefit was shown in the RAS G12 and overall randomized populations. In the small non-G12 subgroup (n=41), PFS HR was 1.38 (95% CI 0.60–3.17) while OS HR was 0.37 (0.15–0.93); these exploratory, imprecise estimates do not establish lack of benefit. Interpretation also requires the open-label design, short follow-up and differential treatment non-initiation (38/252 chemotherapy versus 7/248 daraxonrasib). Check the current prescribing information and patient-specific toxicity risks.
opts.note: The comparator was unconstrained investigator's choice from gemcitabine with nab-paclitaxel, modified FOLFIRINOX, FOLFOX or liposomal irinotecan with fluorouracil, given per local prescribing practice, and its 6.6-month median sits at the low end of published second-line outcomes, so its quality is not auditable from the report. The trial was open label with no crossover; overall survival in an open-label trial remains exposed to differential post-progression therapy, which is not detailed by arm. The sponsor supported the trial and performed and validated the statistical analyses, with five author employees. An overall survival hazard ratio of 0.40 in second-line PDAC is extraordinarily large and should be read with the comparator's 15.1% non-receipt and 11.2% toxicity discontinuation in view.

opts.name: Olaparib maintenance, for germline BRCA1/2 after platinum
opts.when: The POLO trial (n=154 randomised 3:2 from 3,315 screened) randomised patients with metastatic disease and a germline BRCA1/2 mutation who had not progressed after at least 16 weeks of first-line platinum-based therapy to olaparib or placebo. Median progression-free survival by blinded independent central review was 7.4 versus 3.8 months, hazard ratio 0.53 (95% CI 0.35–0.82), P=0.004.
opts.pref: Exactly that population: germline BRCA1/2, platinum-exposed, no progression at 16 weeks. This is the clearest reason to have the germline result early.
opts.avoid: Say the other half. At the interim analysis, at 46% data maturity against a final analysis planned at 69%, there was no overall survival difference — 18.9 versus 18.1 months, hazard ratio 0.91 (0.56–1.46), P=0.68 — there was no difference in health-related quality of life (between-group difference in global health status −2.47, 95% CI −7.27 to 2.33), and grade 3 or worse adverse events were more frequent with olaparib, 40% versus 23%. Objective response was 23% versus 12%, and time to second progression was also non-significant (HR 0.76, 0.46–1.23).
opts.note: Downgraded from A to B. The comparator was placebo, not maintenance chemotherapy or a de-escalated fluoropyrimidine, so the trial establishes that olaparib beats stopping treatment, not that it beats continuing anything — which is the comparison the 16-week decision actually faces. Only 154 of 3,315 screened patients (4.6%) were randomised, and the conditioning step (germline testing plus four months of platinum without progression) is itself the strongest prognostic selection in the trial: a placebo-arm median of 18.1 months in metastatic pancreatic cancer is far above the 6 to 11 months typical of the disease, so these numbers are not comparable with those from unselected trials. Nine placebo patients (15%) received a PARP inhibitor after progression, cited as biasing overall survival toward the null without a sensitivity analysis. The sponsor funded the trial and supplied the companion diagnostic. The page previously quoted the placebo-arm median as 16.1 months; the published figure is 18.1.

opts.name: Pembrolizumab or dostarlimab, for MSI-high or dMMR disease
opts.when: NCCN lists pembrolizumab for MSI-high, dMMR or TMB-high (≥10 mutations/Mb) disease across lines, and dostarlimab for MSI-high or dMMR as subsequent therapy.
opts.pref: The small minority of pancreatic tumours that are MSI-high or mismatch-repair deficient. It is the one alteration on this list that can produce a durable response.
opts.avoid: Do not test for it late. A patient who has exhausted chemotherapy before anyone checked mismatch repair status has lost the opportunity, and the frequency in PDAC is low enough that nobody finds it by clinical suspicion. Graded D because no trial in pancreatic cancer supports either agent: both are tumour-agnostic approvals carried here through the NCCN listing, and no primary report was retrieved or read in full for this depot.

opts.name: Sotorasib or adagrasib, for KRAS G12C
opts.when: NCCN lists both as subsequent therapy options at any performance status. KRAS p.G12C occurs in approximately 1 to 2% of pancreatic cancers.
opts.pref: A previously treated patient with a G12C mutation where daraxonrasib is unavailable. Sotorasib in the pooled phase 1–2 CodeBreaK 100 pancreatic cohort (n=38, all previously treated, about 79% with two or more prior lines): centrally confirmed objective response in 8 of 38 (21%, 95% CI 10–37) with no complete responses, median progression-free survival 4.0 months (2.8–5.6), median overall survival 6.9 months (5.0–9.1). Adagrasib in the KRYSTAL-1 phase 2 non-lung, non-colorectal cohort: objective response in 7 of 21 pancreatic patients (33.3%) by blinded central review, median progression-free survival 5.4 months, median overall survival 8.0 months.
opts.avoid: Downgraded to D, and correct the denominators: these are single-arm results in 38 and 21 pancreatic patients, not in the larger numbers this page previously implied. The sotorasib cohort had no prespecified response benchmark and no hypothesis test at all, so there is no threshold it could have failed, and its 10% to 37% confidence interval is compatible with the under-10% historical second-line benchmark the authors invoke. Adagrasib's prespecified 10% null applies to the pooled tumour-agnostic cohort, not to the pancreatic subgroup, and six patients counted as evaluable by investigators were excluded by central review for having no measurable disease at baseline, moving the denominator in the favourable direction. Median overall survival of 6.9 and 8.0 months in third-line-or-later populations with ECOG 0–1 and a life expectancy requirement is indistinguishable from the natural history of those populations. The allele covers 1% to 2% of the disease, and neither report gives a screening denominator. Do not present them as comparable to the RASolute 302 result.

opts.name: Zenocutuzumab, for NRG1 fusions
opts.when: NCCN lists zenocutuzumab-zbco as a subsequent therapy option for NRG1 fusion-positive disease at performance status 0–2. In the eNRGy basket trial, 36 of 158 patients in the primary efficacy population had pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma, and all 36 were KRAS wild-type: 15 of 36 (42%, 95% CI 25–59) responded by investigator assessment and 16 of 36 (44%, 28–62) by blinded independent central review, with median duration of response 7.4 months (4.0–11.2) investigator-assessed and 9.1 months centrally. Twenty-four of 31 pancreatic patients with baseline data (77%) had a CA 19-9 fall of at least 50%.
opts.pref: A patient with KRAS wild-type disease, where NRG1 fusions are enriched — in a single-institution series the median age of 10 patients with a detectable NRG1 fusion was 48.5 years, and KRAS wild-type status is the practical trigger to look.
opts.avoid: Downgraded to D. Single-arm, 36 pancreatic patients inside a basket trial sized only for the pooled estimate, with a 95% CI of 25% to 59% that cannot distinguish a major advance from a modest one. No progression-free or overall survival is reported for the pancreatic subgroup, so no survival claim can be derived from it. The primary endpoint was investigator-assessed response in an open-label trial with blinded central review only as a secondary endpoint, and the primary efficacy population is a post-enrolment construct — 204 treated patients become 158 evaluable, with exclusions for short follow-up falling disproportionately on early progressors. Only 9 of 47 responses across the whole trial were ongoing at a median follow-up of 7.1 months. Adverse events were mostly grade 1 or 2 with treatment-related grade 3–4 in 7%, so the risk is low — but NRG1 fusions occur in well under 1% of PDAC, no screening denominator is given, and the sponsor designed the trial, analysed the data and drafted the manuscript.

opts.name: An NTRK, RET, BRAF or FGFR-directed agent, by alteration
opts.when: NCCN lists entrectinib, larotrectinib or repotrectinib for NTRK fusion-positive disease; selpercatinib for RET fusions (11 pancreatic patients, at least half with an objective response); dabrafenib with trametinib for BRAF V600E, with ORR 38–47% across the NCI-MATCH subprotocol and the ROAR basket trial; and erdafitinib for FGFR alterations, with response in 10 of 18 pancreatic patients (56%) in RAGNAR.
opts.pref: Rare alterations where the alternative is further cytotoxic chemotherapy in a previously treated patient. Each is a basket-trial or subgroup result in single-digit to low-double-digit pancreatic numbers.
opts.avoid: Downgraded to D: none of these reports was retrieved or read in full for this depot, and all the figures are carried in the NCCN listing supplied to this page. Do not treat the gene as the target. The pancreatic subsets in these trials are tiny — one patient with pancreatic cancer in the larotrectinib analysis, two of three responders among pancreatic patients in the entrectinib trials — and response rates from mixed-tumour baskets do not transfer cleanly to this disease.

old.order: Ordered by the strength of the evidence in pancreatic cancer specifically and by how many patients the alteration reaches, not by response rate. Daraxonrasib is first because it is the only randomised phase 3 result here, and the only one with a survival endpoint — but benefit was demonstrated in both the RAS G12 primary population and the overall population. Non-G12 estimates are exploratory: PFS HR 1.38 (0.60–3.17), OS HR 0.37 (0.15–0.93), n=41. Olaparib is second because POLO is randomised and double-blind but in 154 patients found from 3,315 screened, against placebo rather than continued chemotherapy, and positive only for progression-free survival with no overall survival or quality-of-life difference at interim. Everything below is single-arm, in rare alterations, with pancreatic subsets of 21 to 38 patients, no control groups, and in two cases no prespecified efficacy threshold at all.
old.flagnote: Local approval item 8: what is the local sequence after first-line failure, and where does daraxonrasib sit in it given its availability, cost, the absence of any first-line or perioperative data, and the fact that 15.1% of its comparator arm never received the chemotherapy it was allocated? The group should also agree who owns chasing the molecular report, because the commonest failure in this disease is a result that arrives after the patient is too unwell to act on it. Audit: proportion of metastatic patients with a completed germline result and a completed genomic profile before second line, time from biopsy to report, and proportion of actionable results acted on. [PAYER]

old.t: A chemotherapy holiday or maintenance therapy for a patient doing well on first-line treatment.
old.pref: NCCN offers either for patients who do well on initial therapy. Set the reassessment interval and the trigger for restarting when the holiday begins.
old.avoid: Do not drift into a holiday without a date for the next scan.

old.t: Rucaparib maintenance for germline or somatic BRCA1, BRCA2 or PALB2 variants, as a second option after platinum.
old.pref: A phase 2 trial of maintenance rucaparib after at least 16 weeks of platinum-based chemotherapy in advanced disease with germline or somatic pathogenic variants in BRCA1, BRCA2 or PALB2 reported median progression-free survival of 13.1 months and median duration of response 17.3 months, with no new safety signal.
old.avoid: Downgraded to D: single-arm phase 2 with no control, and the primary report was not retrieved or read in full for this depot — the figures are carried in the NCCN discussion text supplied to this page. The 13.1-month progression-free survival figure cannot be compared with POLO's 7.4 months. Its one advantage over the POLO population is that it included somatic as well as germline variants and PALB2.

The sotorasib cohort had no prespecified response benchmark and no hypothesis test at all, so there is no threshold it could have failed, and its 10% to 37% confidence interval is compatible with the under-10% historical second-line benchmark the authors invoke. Adagrasib's prespecified 10% null applies to the pooled tumour-agnostic cohort, not to the pancreatic subgroup, and six patients counted as evaluable by investigators were excluded by central review for having no measurable disease at baseline, moving the denominator in the favourable direction. Median overall survival of 6.9 and 8.0 months in third-line-or-later populations with ECOG 0–1 and a life expectancy requirement is indistinguishable from the natural history of those populations. The allele covers 1% to 2% of the disease, and neither report gives a screening denominator. Do not present them as comparable to the RASolute 302 result.

opts.name: Zenocutuzumab, for NRG1 fusions
opts.when: NCCN lists zenocutuzumab-zbco as a subsequent therapy option for NRG1 fusion-positive disease at performance status 0–2. In the eNRGy basket trial, 36 of 158 patients in the primary efficacy population had pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma, and all 36 were KRAS wild-type: 15 of 36 (42%, 95% CI 25–59) responded by investigator assessment and 16 of 36 (44%, 28–62) by blinded independent central review, with median duration of response 7.4 months (4.0–11.2) investigator-assessed and 9.1 months centrally. Twenty-four of 31 pancreatic patients with baseline data (77%) had a CA 19-9 fall of at least 50%.
opts.pref: A patient with KRAS wild-type disease, where NRG1 fusions are enriched — in a single-institution series the median age of 10 patients with a detectable NRG1 fusion was 48.5 years, and KRAS wild-type status is the practical trigger to look.
opts.avoid: Downgraded to D. Single-arm, 36 pancreatic patients inside a basket trial sized only for the pooled estimate, with a 95% CI of 25% to 59% that cannot distinguish a major advance from a modest one. No progression-free or overall survival is reported for the pancreatic subgroup, so no survival claim can be derived from it. The primary endpoint was investigator-assessed response in an open-label trial with blinded central review only as a secondary endpoint, and the primary efficacy population is a post-enrolment construct — 204 treated patients become 158 evaluable, with exclusions for short follow-up falling disproportionately on early progressors. Only 9 of 47 responses across the whole trial were ongoing at a median follow-up of 7.1 months. Adverse events were mostly grade 1 or 2 with treatment-related grade 3–4 in 7%, so the risk is low — but NRG1 fusions occur in well under 1% of PDAC, no screening denominator is given, and the sponsor designed the trial, analysed the data and drafted the manuscript.

opts.name: An NTRK, RET, BRAF or FGFR-directed agent, by alteration
opts.when: NCCN lists entrectinib, larotrectinib or repotrectinib for NTRK fusion-positive disease; selpercatinib for RET fusions (11 pancreatic patients, at least half with an objective response); dabrafenib with trametinib for BRAF V600E, with ORR 38–47% across the NCI-MATCH subprotocol and the ROAR basket trial; and erdafitinib for FGFR alterations, with response in 10 of 18 pancreatic patients (56%) in RAGNAR.
opts.pref: Rare alterations where the alternative is further cytotoxic chemotherapy in a previously treated patient. Each is a basket-trial or subgroup result in single-digit to low-double-digit pancreatic numbers.
opts.avoid: Downgraded to D: none of these reports was retrieved or read in full for this depot, and all the figures are carried in the NCCN listing supplied to this page. Do not treat the gene as the target. The pancreatic subsets in these trials are tiny — one patient with pancreatic cancer in the larotrectinib analysis, two of three responders among pancreatic patients in the entrectinib trials — and response rates from mixed-tumour baskets do not transfer cleanly to this disease.

new.order: Ordered by the strength of the evidence in pancreatic cancer specifically and by how many patients the alteration reaches, not by response rate. Daraxonrasib is first because it is the only randomised phase 3 result here, and the only one with a survival endpoint — but benefit was demonstrated in both the RAS G12 primary population and the overall population. Non-G12 estimates are exploratory: PFS HR 1.38 (0.60–3.17), OS HR 0.37 (0.15–0.93), n=41. Olaparib is second because POLO is randomised and double-blind but in 154 patients found from 3,315 screened, against placebo rather than continued chemotherapy, and positive only for progression-free survival with no overall survival or quality-of-life difference at interim. Everything below is single-arm, in rare alterations, with pancreatic subsets of 21 to 38 patients, no control groups, and in two cases no prespecified efficacy threshold at all.
new.flagnote: Local approval item 8: what is the local sequence after first-line failure, and where does daraxonrasib sit in it given its availability, cost, the absence of any first-line or perioperative data, and the fact that 15.1% of its comparator arm never received the chemotherapy it was allocated? The group should also agree who owns chasing the molecular report, because the commonest failure in this disease is a result that arrives after the patient is too unwell to act on it. Audit: proportion of metastatic patients with a completed germline result and a completed genomic profile before second line, time from biopsy to report, and proportion of actionable results acted on. [PAYER]

new.t: A chemotherapy holiday or maintenance therapy for a patient doing well on first-line treatment.
new.pref: NCCN offers either for patients who do well on initial therapy. Set the reassessment interval and the trigger for restarting when the holiday begins.
new.avoid: Do not drift into a holiday without a date for the next scan.

new.t: Rucaparib maintenance for germline or somatic BRCA1, BRCA2 or PALB2 variants, as a second option after platinum.
new.pref: A phase 2 trial of maintenance rucaparib after at least 16 weeks of platinum-based chemotherapy in advanced disease with germline or somatic pathogenic variants in BRCA1, BRCA2 or PALB2 reported median progression-free survival of 13.1 months and median duration of response 17.3 months, with no new safety signal.
new.avoid: Downgraded to D: single-arm phase 2 with no control, and the primary report was not retrieved or read in full for this depot — the figures are carried in the NCCN discussion text supplied to this page. The 13.1-month progression-free survival figure cannot be compared with POLO's 7.4 months. Its one advantage over the POLO population is that it included somatic as well as germline variants and PALB2.

new.t: After progression on gemcitabine-based therapy, consider liposomal irinotecan with fluorouracil/leucovorin for a suitable patient.
new.pref: In NAPOLI-1, 117 combination patients versus 119 concurrent 5-FU/leucovorin controls had median OS 6.1 versus 4.2 months, HR 0.67 (95% CI 0.49–0.92). The trial selected patients with KPS ≥70 and adequate liver function. Reassess performance status, bilirubin/drainage, prior treatment and goals.
new.avoid: The evidence does not establish immediate reuse after irinotecan-containing FOLFIRINOX or NALIRIFOX. Liposomal irinotecan is not interchangeable with conventional irinotecan; use the actual product label and pharmacy-verified dosing. Continue symptom-directed care and consider trials or supportive care when further cytotoxic therapy is unsuitable.

changes.old: Urgent referral route — a same-week slot with chair approval, used routinely here: cholangitis, a rising bilirubin and gastric outlet obstruction are time-critical, and so is a borderline resectable patient whose scan is about to expire. Owner: chair.
changes.new: Urgent clinical care precedes the board: suspected cholangitis requires same-day assessment and timely biliary decompression according to severity; symptomatic gastric outlet obstruction requires prompt assessment, resuscitation and relief as indicated. Escalate immediately for sepsis, dehydration or inability to maintain intake. The board can then coordinate the oncologic plan. Owner: treating clinician and appropriate emergency/endoscopy teams.

changes.old: Ordered by the size and quality of the randomised comparison each regimen achieved, which is a real ranking here — unusually for this page — but a narrower one than the medians suggest. PRODIGE 24 is the only adjuvant trial to report an 18-month difference in median overall survival, and it did so against the then-standard, in a population restricted to age under 80, no cardiac disease, WHO performance status 0 or 1, full surgical recovery and postoperative CA 19-9 below 180 U/mL; nothing in it describes what to do for a patient who has not recovered from a pancreatoduodenectomy, and its 5-year disease-free survival advantage is 7.1 percentage points. Every comparator in this list is adjuvant gemcitabine monotherapy or observation, so the ordering is a chain of comparisons against regimens no pathway would now offer a fit patient, and the two preferred options have never been compared with each other. NCCN also notes how similar the single-agent arms of the older trials were to one another — 22.8 months in the gemcitabine arm of CONKO-001, 20.5 in the gemcitabine-containing arm of RTOG 9704, 20.1 in the bolus fluorouracil arm of ESPAC-1, and 23.6 and 23.0 in the two arms of ESPAC-3 — which is a useful reminder of how small the single-agent era's differences were, and a reminder that those arms were selected very differently on CA 19-9 and age.
changes.new: Choose an adjuvant regimen using guideline recommendations, recovery, fitness and tolerance. PRODIGE-24 randomized mFOLFIRINOX against gemcitabine; ESPAC-4 randomized GemCap against gemcitabine. The two combinations have not been compared head to head, so their different survival medians do not establish a comparative ranking. Trial eligibility and subsequent therapy differ materially.

changes.old: This is the option whose harms the page previously understated. In the 59-patient cohort, Society of Interventional Radiology grade D complications occurred in 6 patients (10%), one patient died three months after embolisation, and 20 of 59 (34%) ultimately required surgery anyway — so embolisation often adds a procedure rather than replacing one. Major complications occurred in 8 of 151 (5.3%) in the systematic review, pooled across emergency and elective indications, so the elective risk is not separately reported. Symptoms were unchanged after embolisation (P=0.134), so do not offer it for pain: it shrank lesions without relieving the complaint. A median post-treatment diameter of 45 mm means the typical embolised lesion sits just below the threshold rather than being eliminated, and the patient re-enters surveillance with an indeterminate lesion and no histology. 'Surgery avoided' is a process endpoint, not a patient outcome, and 31 months is too short to detect malignant transformation. EASL makes residual viable lesion on follow-up imaging an indication for resection.
changes.new: Discuss the mixed elective/emergency cohort explicitly: 6/59 (10%) had major complications; the supplement records 3/36 nonbleeding elective cases and 3/23 bleeding cases. One patient died three months after emergency TAE for haemorrhagic shock, following aspiration pneumonia, with attribution uncertain. Twenty of 59 (34%) later underwent surgery for several indications. Symptoms were reported in 58% before versus 37% within three months (P=.134); durable symptom benefit remains uncertain. Lack of a whole-lesion specimen limits pathological assessment, but some patients had biopsy or previous resection.

changes.source_locator: Full_Text_Review_2026-10-31/Analyst_A_Full_Reaudit_2026-11-01/reviews/metastatic_benign/Source_Reviews/31313827.md; original PDF pp3–8 and SupplementTablesS1–S5
changes.old: EASL reserves embolisation for poor surgical candidates. The data since show 84% surgery avoidance after elective embolisation, on 49 patients from multiple small series, and a fall in median diameter from 76 to 48 mm. Against that: 10% grade D complications, one death three months after emergency TAE for haemorrhagic shock followed by aspiration pneumonia, with uncertain causal attribution, 34% of patients still requiring surgery, no symptom improvement at 3 months (P=0.134), viable tissue and no histology left behind in a disease where 20-40% of presumed adenomas prove to be something else, and a pooled follow-up of 31 months too short to detect transformation. That is a shared decision the programme should endorse or decline explicitly, with the harms disclosed, rather than leave to individual preference.

changes.old: Hepatocellular adenoma is not a standardised exception. The whole indication rests on 142 US transplants over 33 years with 18.3% mortality over a median 62.9 months and 9.0% waitlist mortality in patients of median age 34.5 and median MELD 8 — so almost all of that mortality is treatment-attributable — plus 49 European adenomatosis transplants with three operative deaths, five retransplantations, three fatal recurrences and true transformation in only 17 of 49 explants. The US registry records neither the number nor the size of the adenomas; the European one miscoded a quarter of its cases; neither has a comparison group managed without transplantation; and 61.3% of US recipients received exception points while about a tenth met the stated criteria. Graft stewardship for a benign disease is an institutional judgement, and it should be made with those numbers in front of the committee.
changes.new: HCA is not a standardized MELD exception. Transplant cohorts report selected-recipient outcomes without an untreated comparison: the UNOS analysis had 26 deaths among 142 recipients over median 62.9 months, while its 9.0% waitlist endpoint combined deaths and too-sick removals. These figures do not establish treatment-attributable mortality. The European series assembled 49 confirmed cases; 17 had HCC before or at LT, while the detailed tables record 12 positive explants. It does not establish a 15/64 miscoding rate. Graft stewardship and expected benefit require individual multidisciplinary review.

These figures do not establish treatment-attributable mortality. The European series assembled 49 confirmed cases; 17 had HCC before or at LT, while the detailed tables record 12 positive explants. It does not establish a 15/64 miscoding rate. Graft stewardship and expected benefit require individual multidisciplinary review.

changes.old: Hepatocellular adenoma is not a standardised exception. The whole indication rests on 142 US transplants over 33 years with 18.3% mortality over a median 62.9 months and 9.0% waitlist mortality in patients of median age 34.5 and median MELD 8 — so almost all of that mortality is treatment-attributable — plus 49 European adenomatosis transplants with three operative deaths, five retransplantations, three fatal recurrences and true transformation in only 17 of 49 explants. The US registry records neither the number nor the size of the adenomas; the European one miscoded a quarter of its cases; neither has a comparison group managed without transplantation; and 61.3% of US recipients received exception points while about a tenth met the stated criteria. Graft stewardship for a benign disease is an institutional judgement, and it should be made with those numbers in front of the committee.

changes.old: Revised on 7 October 2026 after a full-text read of the depot. All 46 papers behind this page were read in full and abstracted, each with the authors' stated limitations and an independent critique recorded, and every evidence string on the page was checked against that abstraction. Fifty-eight evidence strings changed, across 119 fields. Six are corrections large enough to change what the page tells a surgeon, and they are set out in the limited-evidence section: that 5 cm is a convention rather than a derived threshold, which the page now states in the size assessment itself and grades D; that the six-month decision point is mistimed, because only 8.5-15.3% of adenomas over 5 cm have regressed below 5 cm at 26 weeks against 58.5% eventually at a median 104 weeks with no complication during that follow-up; that the apparent size gradient in the 122-patient, 365-adenoma French series is largely a per-lesion artefact of a resect-everything policy whose sub-2 cm stratum is incidental microadenomas found inside specimens removed for a larger lesion; that transarterial embolisation caused one reported death and left 34% of patients still requiring surgery, where the earlier draft stated that no deaths were reported; that the 23.8% occult-carcinoma figure the earlier draft attributed to a US male resection series is not supported and has been withdrawn, the supported figure being 4 transformations in 27 male adenomas; and that the positional and vascular bleeding effect sizes the earlier draft attributed to a prospective imaging cohort could not be confirmed and have been withdrawn, with the composite-trigger proposal and approval item 7 left explicitly undecided until someone reads that paper's positional analysis. Grades were revised where the critique warranted it rather than from study design alone: the 5 cm resection trigger, the 6-month reimaging interval, the composite positional trigger and thermal ablation were all downgraded, and the pregnancy recommendation for lesions under 5 cm moved from B to C because zero ruptures in 51 pregnancies has an upper 95% confidence bound of about 7% and both pregnancy cohorts were pre-filtered by the rule they are used to relax. Six papers newly obtained for this revision have been added: the French multicentre bleeding cohort that modelled size continuously and found no threshold (Ann Surg 2021, PMID 34334644); the Dutch nationwide audit of diagnostic accuracy in resections for presumed adenoma (Hepatol Commun 2022, PMID 36324268); the Korean nationwide clinical, radiological and pathological series (Liver Int 2024, PMID 39526315); the contemporary surveillance-dominant natural-history cohort (Eur J Gastroenterol Hepatol 2026, PMID 42214026); the narrative review presenting the hepatocellular adenoma and carcinoma classification of the WHO 6th edition (Virchows Arch 2026, PMID 42678415), which is cited throughout as a review of that classification and not as the classification itself, which has not been read for this page; and the imaging-surveillance meta-analysis already present from the first draft and now read in full (Abdom Radiol 2026, PMID 41364225). One paper named in the gap scan was not obtained and is not cited anywhere: McDermott 2021 (PMID 34687281). Elfrink 2021 (PMID 33478819), the Dutch nationwide comparison of 415 laparoscopic and open resections that clinical decision 4 describes through the Italian guideline, has since been read in full. Volume and page numbers were not available for the five newly added references and have not been invented; each is cited by journal, year, title and PMID, with that limitation stated in the reference entry. Two references remain cited from abstract only, because they are not in the full-text depot: the review of ruptured hepatocellular adenoma management (Dig Surg 2010, PMID 20357452), which supports the acute-haemorrhage sequence in clinical decision 5, and the French-language review of hepatic lesions in altered liver vascularisation (Rev Med Liege 2025, PMID 39950525), which supports the vascular-liver-disease string in clinical decision 8. Both of those decision points should be read as the weakest-sourced on the page. Where the earlier draft carried a figure that the full-text abstraction does not contain and that figure bore argumentative weight, it has been replaced with a depot-supported figure or removed and the removal disclosed; purely descriptive detail from the abstract-only draft has in a few places been left in place, and anyone re-reading this page against the sources should expect to find such detail rather than assume it was verified. The page was originally built from EASL Clinical Practice Guidelines on the management of benign liver tumours (J Hepatol 2016;65:386-398), which remains the last full guideline for this disease; the ACG Clinical Guideline on Focal Liver Lesions (Am J Gastroenterol 2024;119:1235-1271); the Italian multisociety benign liver lesions guideline of 2022, which the full-text read shows to be the only adenoma guideline built on a formal GRADE Evidence-to-Decision framework and which grades every size-based adenoma recommendation very low quality of evidence (D), conditional; the French multisociety guidance of 2021, whose every adenoma recommendation is graded C1, C2 or D2; the Nault molecular classification of hepatocellular adenoma (Gastroenterology 2017;152:880-894.e6) and the Rebouissou CTNNB1 genotype-phenotype study (Hepatology 2016;64:2047-2061) for subtype and mutation risk; and the primary literature since 2016 on subtype-specific risk, male adenomas, surveillance outcomes, embolisation, thermal ablation, pregnancy, adenomatosis and transplantation, all of it listed in the reference library with PMIDs verified individually against PubMed on 6 October 2026. The transplant assessment and quick reference 4 come from the local UTHealth Houston Hepatic Adenoma Liver Transplant Protocol V3, policy review date 21 September 2026, which is the authority for that assessment and for nothing else on the page; the board and front-door operating content draws on the UTHealth Houston / Memorial Hermann Master Workup and Staging CPG and its hepatic adenoma staging row. Allocation statements are reproduced from that protocol and have not been independently checked against the live OPTN Policy 9.4 and 9.5 postings or the December 2025 transplant-oncology review-board guidance; the protocol marks several of them VERIFY and they remain unverified here. The 2025 UK NHSBT Liver Advisory Group guidance has now been read: it assigns patients with benign liver tumours to four eligibility categories by consensus with no underlying cohort, and because it does not state how adenoma size, number, subtype or prior intervention map onto those categories, its criteria are still not paraphrased on this page. One earlier source gap is recorded for completeness: the file supplied as the European adenomatosis source contained an unrelated French conference paper with no adenoma content, so the adenomatosis evidence here comes instead from the Tours long-term observational cohort (J Hepatol 2019;71:1184-1192), the European Liver Transplant Registry adenomatosis series (Liver Transpl 2016;22:516-526) and EASL's own multiple-lesion section. This page remains a draft. Unlike the five existing disease pages it transcribes no ratified system roadmap, because none exists for hepatocellular adenoma: outside the transplant assessment, every position on it is a proposal assembled from published guidelines and primary literature and awaiting multidisciplinary and institutional local approval. The full-text read has made the page more honest about the strength of its own recommendations; it has not made any of them policy. It is not active clinical policy, it does not replace clinician judgement, and every numeric criterion must be verified against the current source before use.

changes.old: Revised on 7 October 2026 after a full-text read of this page's reference depot. Twenty-eight of the 33 indexed papers were read in full and abstracted to a fixed schema recording setting, inclusion and exclusion criteria, results, the authors' own stated limitations, an independent critique and a bottom line, and every evidence string, number and grade on the page was checked against that abstraction. Thirty-nine evidence strings were changed and thirteen grades were downgraded; the assessment structure, ids, names and tone values are unchanged, five previously empty recommendation slots were filled from depot papers that the first draft indexed but did not cite, the limited-evidence section grew from 12 items to 25 and the approvals list from 10 to 15. Originally built from the programme-supplied extraction of NCCN Neuroendocrine and Adrenal Tumors (version not stated in the extracted text; its most recent references, including the MEN1 guideline of June 2025, place it at v3.2025 or later) as the spine, with the NANETS 2020 consensus paper on the surgical management of pancreatic neuroendocrine tumours (Pancreas 2020;49:1-33) as the main surgical source, and the ENETS 2023 guidance papers for nonfunctioning pancreatic NET (J Neuroendocrinol 2023;35:e13343), for functioning pancreatic NET syndromes (e13318) and for digestive neuroendocrine carcinoma (e13249). Grading follows the WHO 2019 criteria as reproduced in the NCCN pathology principles. Liver metastases are out of scope throughout and hand off by name to the NELM pathway, which carries the hepatic decisions and the primary-resection question in metastatic disease. What the full-text read changed most is the observation-versus-resection assessment. The ENETS position on the 1-2 cm band, previously taken from the abstract and from how NANETS and the ASPEN investigators report it, was wrong: the full text observes 1 cm or less, personalises 1-2 cm and strongly recommends surgery above 2 cm or with duct dilation, and the page and quick-reference table are corrected. Sadot 2016's inclusion band was 3 cm or less rather than 2 cm, so the paper most often cited for the 2 cm threshold never tested it; a quarter of its observation arm crossed to surgery and remain in it by intention to treat; the patients never operated were followed a median of 33 months against a median time to recurrence of 5.1 years in the resected arm; its metastasis-free survival advantage for observation is an endpoint artefact; and 51% of observed tumours grew. ASPEN's 20% rate of aggressive histology comes only from its 94 resected patients, a denominator selected for size, duct dilatation, age, anxiety and surgeon preference, and no comparison between strategies was performed; its metastasis rate is printed as 0.08% when 4 of 500 is 0.8%. In PANDORA, six of the eight progressing patients refused the protocol-mandated operation, so the protocol was not tested. Gratian 2014 is a National Cancer Data Base analysis rather than SEER, and the registry excludes tumours coded benign, which removes exactly the indolent lesions a surveillance policy concerns; its 33% nodal figure for sub-5 mm tumours rests on a 94-patient band in a variable missing in 45% of the cohort. The 2025 MEN1 best-practice recommendations contribute the only systematic comparison that exists: across 37 studies and 1,814 patients, surgery and surveillance for lesions under 2 cm showed no difference in metastasis or mortality at low to very low GRADE certainty. And Hashim 2014, Zheng-Pywell 2022 and Makris 2023 all draw observation-versus-resection conclusions from cohorts in which every patient was resected, which is recorded on the page as a structural defect of the nodal-risk literature rather than as a caveat. Still cited from abstract only, because no new papers were obtained in this pass: the AACE consensus statement on MEN1 of March 2025 (PMID 40232217) and the 2021 international consensus statement on the pancreas in MEN1 (PMID 32971521). Both are labelled as abstract-only wherever they are cited, and their numeric criteria must be confirmed before use. The NANETS 2020 surgical consensus and the ENETS functioning-syndromes and neuroendocrine carcinoma guidance papers were not part of the full-text depot and remain the programme-supplied guideline sources; a list of figures quoted from the NANETS text with no primary paper in the depot is recorded in the limited-evidence section and each is labelled where it is used. There is still no ratified Memorial Hermann roadmap behind this page and no alignment worksheet. It remains a draft, assembled from guidelines and primary literature, pending multidisciplinary and institutional governance review. It is not active clinical policy, it does not replace clinician judgement, and every numeric criterion on it must be verified against the current source before use.

changes.old: Revised on 7 October 2026 after a full-text read of the whole 27-paper reference depot for this page, with each paper abstracted to its results, the authors' stated limitations and an independent critique. The first draft had been built from abstracts and guideline summaries; four of the five documents that set the thresholds on this page — the international evidence-based Kyoto guidelines (Ohtsuka 2024, PMID 38182527), Fukuoka 2017 (PMID 28735806), Fukuoka 2012 (PMID 22687371) and the original Sendai consensus (PMID 16327281) — had not previously been checked against in full, and reading them changed the page's spine rather than its structure. What changed most: Kyoto 2024's malignancy rates of 31% and 62% are prevalences in resected specimens and the document itself now states that the real rate across all branch-duct IPMNs is much lower without quantifying it, so neither figure appears on this page as a surveillance risk; Kyoto retained the 5 mm mural nodule and 10 mm main-duct thresholds in the same passage that reports odds ratios of 1.19 to 3.16 and 1.06 to 1.76 for them and an odds ratio of 7.90 for a 10 mm nodule; the 2.5 mm per year growth threshold was adopted because 2.5 was the value reported most frequently among candidates spanning 0.96 to 3.5; no sensitivity, specificity or predictive value is published for any risk tier three guideline generations in; surgical mortality and cost-effectiveness appear nowhere in the IAP line of guidelines or the European guideline, so those numbers have been assembled from ACG, AGA, PROPAN and the surgical series; the only large external validation found that the 30 mm threshold did not stratify risk (subdistribution hazard ratio 1.75, 95% CI 1.00 to 3.08, against 2.07, 1.38 to 3.10, at 20 to 29 mm); and the three cohorts behind the stopping debate are shown on clinical decision 9 to differ in baseline selection, in conditioning on survival to 5 years, in whether high-grade dysplasia is counted as an event against an invasive-cancer-only comparator, and in how long they observed past the 5-year mark, which accounts for their opposite conclusions. Two numbers flagged in the first draft as needing verification are now resolved from the full texts: the ACG 2 to 3 cm surveillance band is MRI or EUS every 6 to 12 months for 3 years then yearly for 4, and the Kyoto cyst-fluid glucose threshold is 50 mg/dL with 93% sensitivity and 89% specificity. Three claims in the first draft were wrong and have been corrected: Kyoto does quantify needle-tract and peritoneal seeding (0.3%, and 2.3% against 4.4%, P=0.403); Kyoto and the European guideline do give operating characteristics for serum CA 19-9; and the European guideline does not merely omit needle-based confocal laser endomicroscopy from its algorithm but recommends against it at GRADE 1C. Grades were lowered where the full text showed a threshold to be a consensus value rather than a derived one, and the reason is stated in each note. The current narrative review of the field (Gardner 2024, PMID 38442782) is cited only for its cost figures, its population-versus-individual framing and its list of circumstances in which stopping is uncontroversial: its table of branch-duct transformation rates pools structurally incompatible denominators into an apparent 3.5 to 5.5% agreement, and its guideline-comparison table misreports several criteria, so no rate and no criterion on this page comes from it. Three sources on this page were not in the depot and are not full-text verified to the same standard: NCCN Pancreatic Adenocarcinoma Version 1.2026, from the extracted text supplied to the programme with its Discussion dated 6 August 2026, which has no cyst algorithm of its own, cites Kyoto 2024 as the international standard, cites the superseded 2013 European consensus statement rather than the 2018 evidence-based guideline, and directs the reader to the most recent available guideline; the 2013 European consensus statement itself (PMID 23415799), listed because it is the document NCCN reaches for — outside the depot at this revision, it has since been read in full; and the WHO 5th edition entity definitions, used but not re-verified against the current online edition. This is a first draft and there is no ratified roadmap behind it. Unlike the programme's five existing disease roadmaps, this pathway transcribes no approved institutional document — there is no local pancreatic cyst protocol in the source set — and it takes no institutional position of its own. Where the four guidelines disagree, which on this disease is on almost everything that matters, the page shows the disagreement and refers the choice to the nineteen local approval items in the approvals section; the order of options in any assessment reflects guideline standing or the spine chosen for this page, never a demonstrated advantage. It is not active clinical policy, it does not replace clinician judgement, and every numeric criterion must be verified against the current source before use.
