changes.old: This is a second draft, revised on 7 October 2026 after a full-text read of the paper depot behind it. There is still no ratified Memorial Hermann roadmap for ampullary tumours, no alignment worksheet behind it, and no institutional position has been taken on any of the fifteen items in the approvals list — the page is a proposal for a multidisciplinary group to argue with, not a statement of practice. What the full-text read changed. Twenty-eight of the thirty-five cited papers were read in full and abstracted with their authors' stated limitations and an independent critique, and the revision moved the page in three material ways. First, ESPAC-3 can no longer be cited as establishing adjuvant benefit in ampullary cancer: the trial was never powered for its ampullary subgroup, reports no hypothesis test for ampullary-only survival anywhere, and the ampullary medians of 40.6, 57.8 and 70.8 months appear without a P value; its primary analysis was negative (hazard ratio 0.86, 95% CI 0.66–1.11, P=0.25), its adjusted analysis (0.75, 0.57–0.98, P=0.03) adjusted for four variables on two of which the observation arm was prognostically worse at baseline, and in its 96 intrapancreatic bile duct patients chemotherapy was numerically worse than observation. Adjuvant chemotherapy remains on the page and is now graded C and offered as a reasonable choice rather than a demonstrated benefit. Second, the subtype question has been rewritten as an asymmetric dispute rather than a tie: the reproducibility study is the ceiling on all of it (κ 0.39, all five observers agreeing in 23% of 232 cases, 40% of tumours mixed, pure intestinal only 6%, survival differing only after the mixed cases were force-assigned, and the subtype failing multivariable analysis at P=0.39), and of the two adjuvant cohorts the positive one allocated treatment at tumour board by prognosis with no adjustment of any kind and reports a whole-cohort result running the other way (hazard ratio 1.124, P=0.608) while the negative one propensity-matched on the actual selection drivers and handled immortal time bias — so the divergence is explained by cohort and method rather than by chance, although the negative result is still underpowered to exclude a modest benefit. Third, the European comparison of papillectomy with surgical ampullectomy is now read for its indication finding first: final histology was neither adenoma nor adenocarcinoma in 24.2% of papillectomies and 14.8% of surgical ampullectomies while advanced disease was found in 10.9% and 36.6%, so roughly a third of the procedures in both arms were done for the wrong indication; papillectomy R0 for adenoma falls from 80.2% to 65.9% once index-session ablation is counted as a probable R2 resection; and papillectomy failed in roughly two-thirds of T1 cancers. Borrowed evidence. ESPAC-4 and PRODIGE-24 are trials of resected pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma that excluded nonductal tumours by design and report no ampullary patients; the page now says so wherever it uses them, as it does for the preoperative biliary drainage trial (cancer of the pancreatic head, plastic stents, no ampullary subgroup), BILCAP (biliary tract), ABC-02 (advanced biliary tract, 20 ampullary patients; subgroup OS HR 0.62 (0.21–1.82)), X-ACT (colon) and the randomised evidence against extended lymphadenectomy (pancreatic). Cited from abstract only. Five papers were sought and not obtained for this revision. Three of them — the 91-patient malignancy prediction cohort (23442830), the EUS preoperative evaluation series (30834717) and the 14-patient ampullary neuroendocrine tumour series (27457864) — have since been read in full; the other two, the National Cancer Database node-yield analysis (PMID 38353072) and the intraductal ultrasound and transpapillary biopsy series (22319960), are still cited from abstract only, and every string that uses them says so. BILCAP (30922733) and ABC-02 (20375404) were also not part of the full-text read and are quoted from their abstracts and from guideline text. Guideline sources, unchanged from the first draft. The programme-supplied machine-converted extraction of the NCCN Ampullary Adenocarcinoma guideline, which carries no version string and which misstates ESPAC-3 on its adjuvant systemic-therapy page while stating it correctly in its discussion (see nonpm, and approvals item 10) — the full-text read confirms that discrepancy from the trial side; the NCCN Pancreatic Adenocarcinoma extraction for the margin, specimen and lymphadenectomy questions the two diseases share; the Brescia PERIPAN international multidisciplinary consensus guidelines of 29 July 2025 for the anatomic definitions, the subtype definitions, the biopsy and specimen-handling recommendations and the reflex mismatch-repair position; the ESGE guideline on endoscopic management of ampullary tumours of 2021 and the ESGE polyposis guideline of 2019 for the endoscopic and familial decision points; and AJCC 8th edition staging as reproduced in NCCN. Every PMID in refs was verified against PubMed on 6 October 2026 to confirm it resolves to the paper cited. Readers should know that nine of eleven main ESGE ampullary recommendations are strong on low-quality evidence, that almost every PERIPAN recommendation is low evidence or expert opinion with its promised AGREE II quality score and audience vote never reported, and that PERIPAN's 30% threshold for the mixed subtype has no stated derivation. Where the sources disagree — on whether subtype should direct adjuvant therapy, on surveillance intervals by Spigelman stage, on whether mismatch-repair and molecular testing is reflex, indication-driven or discouraged, on the minimum node yield, and on what to do with an invasive carcinoma found in a margin-negative papillectomy specimen — the page shows the disagreement and places the choice in a flagnote and in approvals rather than resolving it. Evidence strings carry both halves of every result. Grades fell in eleven places on this revision and rose nowhere, and each downgrade is explained in the note on the string it belongs to; no recommendation was removed, because the roadmap's positions stand and the page's job is to say how well supported they are. Grades are deliberately low across the benign end of the pathway: most of what is done there rests on retrospective series and expert consensus, and grade D is used where that is the truth. This page does not replace clinician judgement, and every numeric criterion must be verified against the current source before use.

changes.old: Where the cyst type is genuinely unresolved, or where a result indicating advanced neoplasia would move a borderline patient to theatre. In a prospective study of specimens from 31 institutions, 1,887 of 1,933 (98%) were adequate: MAPK-pathway or GNAS mutations gave 90% sensitivity and 100% specificity for a mucinous cyst (PPV 100%, NPV 77%), against 77% and 92% for increased fluid viscosity and 73% and 94% for CEA above 192 ng/mL. Adding TP53, SMAD4 or mTOR-pathway alterations at allele frequencies equal to the driver gave 87% sensitivity and 99% specificity for advanced neoplasia (PPV 98%, NPV 92%), rising to 89% and 98% with CTNNB1 (PPV 97%, NPV 93%) and to 93% sensitivity at 95% specificity with cytology added. VHL alterations identified serous cystadenomas (71% sensitivity, 100% specificity) and MEN1 with loss of heterozygosity of TP53, SMAD4, PTEN or RNF43 identified cystic neuroendocrine tumours (68%, 98%; MEN1 alone, 27% and 100%).

changes.source_locator: Full_Text_Review_2026-10-31/Analyst_A_Full_Reaudit_2026-11-01/reviews/pancreatic_ampullary/Source_Reviews/PMID_37230894.md; Pflüger2023Figure5; Full_Text_Review_2026-10-31/Analyst_B/batches/B21_pcyst_roadmap/reviews/R3/36209796.md, Table2
changes.old: Read the molecular figures with their denominator: in the prospective multi-institutional study 1,887 of 1,933 specimens were adequate, 1,216 of 1,832 patients had follow-up, and surgical pathology existed for only 251 (14%) — so the performance estimates rest on the operated minority, and the decision to operate was informed by the molecular result. The allele-frequency rules that lift specificity to 98 to 100% were derived in the same group's earlier cohorts, and every specimen was processed in the one lead laboratory, so 'multi-institutional' describes where the fluid came from. The panel is one laboratory's assay charged at $750 per specimen, not a class of test, and another laboratory's panel does not inherit these numbers. Note the gap between the developers' prospective figures and Kyoto 2024's pooled figures for the same grade markers, which is wide enough to matter at the bedside, and that the two glucose meta-analyses pool largely the same seven primary studies and are not independent of each other. Every threshold on this table was fitted in the data that report its performance — CEA at 192, amylase at 250, the glucose cut-offs pooled across 30, 41 and 50 mg/dL, and the molecular allele-frequency rules. No guideline requires molecular testing. CEA cannot grade dysplasia and both ACG and Kyoto say so; a negative result on any test on this table returns the patient to the interval their size and features already indicate, and does not justify a longer one.

changes.old: Read the limits honestly, and do not apply the headline figure to the cyst in front of you without checking which lesion it came from. KRAS, BRAF or GNAS alterations were found in 159 of 167 IPMNs (95%) but KRAS in only 9 of 19 mucinous cystic neoplasms (47%), so for a non-communicating body or tail cyst in a middle-aged woman the sensitivity is 47%, not 90%. Surgical pathology existed for only 251 of 1,832 tested patients (14%), or 251 of the 1,216 with follow-up (21%), so the performance figures rest on the operated minority, and the decision to operate was itself informed by the molecular result — which depresses the measured sensitivity of the comparator criteria and inflates that of the panel. The allele-frequency rules that lift specificity to 98 to 100% were derived in the same group's earlier single-centre cohorts and the confirmation cohort came from the same molecular archive, and every specimen was processed in the one lead laboratory, so 'multi-institutional' describes where the fluid came from and not where it was analysed. The panel is that laboratory's assay rather than a class of test, charged at $750 per specimen in the 2018 series, so another laboratory's panel does not inherit these numbers. Kyoto 2024's own pooled figures for the grade markers are much weaker — TP53, SMAD4, CDKN2A and PIK3CA alterations at 9 to 39% sensitivity and 92 to 98% specificity — so a negative molecular result is not a reason to stand down. Nine resected IPMNs were driver-negative preoperatively and positive on the specimen, which makes the 90% sensitivity partly a property of the aspiration rather than of the sequencing. Coverage must be confirmed in writing before this enters routine practice. [PAYER]

changes.old: Downgraded to D from C after the full-text read: the threshold is a consensus value selected by frequency of publication, not a derived cut-off, however well the resulting variable performs in one cohort. There is also a signal the guidelines do not use. In the 804 Tokyo patients followed beyond 5 years, the increase in main pancreatic duct diameter over the first 5 years predicted later carcinoma (SHR 1.71 per mm, 1.44 to 2.03) while the increase in cyst size did not (1.46, 0.96 to 2.20) — and Kyoto 2024 considered adding 'increase in size of MPD' as a worrisome feature and rejected it for lack of evidence. Median duct increase over those 5 years was 0.2 mm (range −2.0 to 9.0), so this is a measurement that demands a consistent protocol. Whether this programme records duct growth as well as cyst growth is an approvals item.

changes.source_locator: Full_Text_Review_2026-10-31/Analyst_B/batches/B21_pcyst_roadmap/reviews/R6/31473224.md; Oyama2020Table4 and Results pp5–8; R8-R8-D06
changes.old: There are four definitions, not three: Kyoto 2.5 mm per year, ACG more than 3 mm per year, Fukuoka 2017 5 mm over 2 years, the European guideline 5 mm per year. Kyoto adopted 2.5 because it was the value most frequently reported among candidates spanning 0.96 to 3.5 mm per year, which is a choice by vote frequency rather than performance. None has published measurement reproducibility and 2.5 mm is inside the range over which two readers can disagree. Separately, in the one cohort that measured both, the increase in main pancreatic duct diameter over 5 years predicted later carcinoma (SHR 1.71 per mm, 1.44 to 2.03) and the increase in cyst size did not (1.46, 0.96 to 2.20) — and no guideline records duct growth, Kyoto having considered and rejected it for lack of evidence.

changes.old: Ordered from the most conservative to the most permissive. No winner is picked here and none should be read in. The three cohorts differ on four things, and those four differences account for the opposite conclusions, so the order reflects how much imaging each position commits the programme to and not any comparison of outcomes. First, baseline selection: the two cohorts that found a large excess admitted cysts that already had or went on to develop worrisome features — 36% of the US cohort had worrisome features or high-risk stigmata at some point, and the Tokyo cohort counted a mural nodule developing during follow-up as an outcome (subdistribution hazard ratio 11.5, 4.49 to 29.6) — while the cohort that found no excess excluded those cysts by design at entry and again at 5 years. Second, conditioning on survival: all three report a denominator of patients who reached 5 years without being resected or diagnosed, which continuously purges the cohort of its highest-risk members in whichever direction the authors are arguing. Third, the numerator: the two high estimates count high-grade dysplasia as an event against invasive-cancer-only registry comparators, which is what produces standardised incidence ratios of 18.8 and 10.8, while the low estimate counts invasive cancer only, and 14 of its 40 cancers were diagnosed radiologically or on aspiration rather than pathologically. Fourth, observation past the mark: the two high estimates watched for a median of 107 months each beyond 5 years, the low estimate for 85. Nothing about biology separates these papers that is not also explained by how they were built.
changes.new: These are different surveillance cohorts, not a randomized comparison of stopping rules. Selection at baseline and at the five-year landmark, endpoint definitions, follow-up duration and competing mortality differ. In Oyama, the SIR was 10.8 for the full 1,404-patient cohort but 5.8 (95% CI 3.7–7.9) among 804 patients followed beyond five years. The reported 107 months describes total follow-up, not an additional 107 months after year five. Decisions to continue or stop require the patient's current risk, life expectancy, surgical fitness and preferences.

changes.old: Pick one and write it down. The schedules differ by a factor of three or more in imaging per patient-decade for the same cyst, and the stopping rules differ by the whole remainder of a life. The three cohorts behind the stopping debate reach opposite conclusions, and four structural differences account for it. Baseline selection: the two that found a large excess admitted cysts that already had or developed worrisome features — 36% of the 577-patient US cohort at some point, and a mural nodule developing during follow-up carried a hazard ratio of 11.5 in the Tokyo cohort — while the 3,844-patient international cohort excluded them at entry and again at 5 years. Conditioning on survival: each reports a denominator of patients who reached 5 years unresected and undiagnosed (363 of 577, 804 of 1,404, 1,617 of 3,844). Numerator: the two high estimates count high-grade dysplasia as an event against invasive-cancer-only registry comparators, which is what gives standardised incidence ratios of 18.8 (9.7–32.8) and 10.8 (8.2–13.3), and the first drops to 15.6 (7.5–28.7) when restricted to invasive disease; the low estimate counts invasive cancer only and 14 of its 40 cancers were radiologic or aspiration diagnoses rather than pathological. Observation past the mark: 107 months and 107 months against 85. In the low-estimate cohort the standardised incidence ratio after 5 years of stability was 1.12 (0.23–3.39) in patients 75 or older and 0.95 (0.11–3.42) in those 65 or older with lesions of 15 mm or less — from 3 and 2 cancers — while stable cysts above 30 mm carried 10.29 (4.12–21.21), and the ratio falls with age because the comparator population's incidence rises, so the rule licenses stopping in the group at highest absolute risk. Kyoto provides an IPMN-specific framework and does not supply a universal schedule for every pancreatic cyst type.

changes.old: A direct correction. The earlier version stated that no deaths were reported in either the 59-patient cohort or the 151-patient systematic review. The full-text read records that one patient in the 59-patient cohort died three months after embolisation, that Society of Interventional Radiology grade D complications occurred in 6 of 59 (10%), and that 20 of 59 (34%) ultimately required surgery anyway — so embolisation frequently adds a procedure rather than replacing one. Symptoms were unchanged after the procedure (P=0.134) despite median diameter falling from 76 mm to 48 mm at 5.5 months and 45 mm at 27.4 months, which means the benefit rests entirely on a surrogate: it changes the imaging more reliably than it changes the patient. A median post-treatment diameter of 45 mm leaves the typical lesion just below the threshold rather than eliminated, with no histology, re-entering surveillance. Surgery avoided is a process endpoint, the 84% elective figure rests on 49 patients drawn from multiple small series with no common protocol, the 5.3% major-complication rate pools emergency with elective cases so the elective risk is not separately reported, and a pooled median follow-up of 31 months is too short to detect malignant transformation in a lesion that was never removed. Given that 20-40% of resected presumed adenomas prove to be something else, an unknown fraction of those patients were embolised for focal nodular hyperplasia. None of this removes embolisation from the page; all of it belongs in the consent conversation, and approval item 5 should be decided with it in view.
changes.new: The 59-patient cohort combined elective and emergency embolisation. Major complications occurred in 6/59 (10%); one patient died three months after emergency treatment for haemorrhagic shock following aspiration pneumonia, with attribution uncertain. Twenty of 59 later underwent surgery for several indications. Symptoms fell from 58% to 37% within three months (P=.134); this does not establish no symptom benefit, and long-term benefit remains uncertain. Imaging denominators changed over time and some patients had biopsy or earlier resection. Discuss these limitations when comparing TAE with surgery.

changes.old: Two series and a review, all retrospective and all heavily selected. UNOS 1987-2020: 199 patients listed with crude waitlist mortality of 18 of 199 (9.0%); 142 transplanted at a median age 34.5, 79.6% female, 22.5% children, median laboratory MELD at transplant 8 — these were not patients with failing livers; 127 of 142 (89.4%) had no carcinoma; death in 26 of 142 (18.3%) over a median 62.9 months, with patient survival 94.2%, 89.7% and 86.3% at 1, 3 and 5 years and graft survival 89.3%, 84.1% and 80.0%. Because the recipients were young with preserved liver function, almost all of that mortality is attributable to the treatment rather than to the disease. 61.3% received MELD exception points although only 6.3% had glycogen storage disease and 4.9% a listing carcinoma codiagnosis. The registry records neither the number nor the size of the adenomas, so the largest experience of the most radical treatment in this disease contains no data on the variable the rest of the pathway turns on. European registry, adenomatosis: 49 transplants with true malignant transformation in 17 explants (35%), three operative deaths, five retransplantations and three fatal carcinoma recurrences — the series documents important mortality and graft harms, but comparison with a separate conservatively managed cohort cannot estimate transplant-attributable mortality or net benefit; and 15 of 64 registry-coded cases were not adenomatosis at all once verified. The accompanying systematic review of 99 published cases reports 6.0% mortality against 18.3% in UNOS, a threefold disagreement the authors attribute to publication bias in their own review
changes.new: Chiche: 49 confirmed recipients; 17 had HCC before or at LT, with 12 positive explants in detailed tables, four negative after prior HCC and one unavailable. Three operative deaths, five retransplants and three fatal HCC recurrences. The study does not establish a 15/64 miscoding rate or a treatment-attributable mortality fraction.

changes.old: Grade D, and the governance question behind approval item 10. In UNOS from 1987 to 2020, 199 patients were listed with crude waitlist mortality of 18 of 199 (9.0%) and 142 were transplanted at a median age of 34.5 with a median laboratory MELD of 8 — young people with preserved liver function — of whom 127 (89.4%) had no carcinoma; death occurred in 26 of 142 (18.3%) over a median 62.9 months, with 5-year patient survival 86.3% and graft survival 80.0%. Because the recipients were not in liver failure, these observational data cannot determine how much mortality was attributable to treatment rather than underlying disease or comorbidity. 61.3% received MELD exception points although only 6.3% had glycogen storage disease and 4.9% a listing carcinoma codiagnosis, so the exception pathway functions as a discretionary route rather than a rule. And the registry records neither the number nor the size of the adenomas, so the largest experience of the most radical treatment in this disease contains no data on the variable the rest of the pathway turns on. The European adenomatosis registry found true malignant transformation in only 17 of 49 explants (35%) with three operative deaths, five retransplantations and three fatal carcinoma recurrences — roughly one patient in eight dying of the treatment or its failure, against a 2.5% ten-year transformation rate in adenomatosis managed conservatively — and 15 of 64 registry-coded cases proved not to be adenomatosis at all on verification. The accompanying systematic review of 99 published cases reports 6.0% mortality against UNOS's 18.3%, a threefold disagreement its own authors attribute to publication bias in their review. Neither dataset has a comparison group managed without transplantation, so the claim of excellent outcomes in well-selected patients is unfalsifiable from these data. The 2025 UK national guidance assigns patients to four eligibility categories by consensus with no cohort behind them and no reference to beta-catenin or sonic hedgehog status.
changes.new: The UNOS cohort and European adenomatosis series describe highly selected recipients and cannot estimate benefit versus nontransplant care. UNOS reported 26/142 deaths over median 62.9 months; deaths had diverse causes. Chiche identified 17 patients with HCC before or at LT, not 17 uniformly positive explants. These reports support careful counseling and graft stewardship but not attribution of nearly all mortality to treatment.

changes.old: Not a clinical position but a methodological one that bears on every number this page quotes from a registry, including the local protocol's transplant evidence and any future audit. In the European series, 15 of 64 cases coded as liver adenomatosis in the registry proved not to be adenomatosis once the contributing centres verified them — a quarter of entries wrong. The UNOS analysis depends on the same kind of coding plus a free-text search on the fragment aden, with no case-level verification, so its cohort definition is weaker than the one already shown to fail. The same problem appears clinically rather than administratively: half of presumed male adenomas are reclassified on expert pathology review, 43% of Dutch resections for presumed adenoma had their diagnosis changed, and 27% of referred sub-5 cm lesions in a prospective cohort were focal nodular hyperplasia. The implication for this programme's own registry is that the concordance field — preoperative diagnosis against final pathology — is not an audit nicety but the field that makes every other field interpretable.
changes.new: Registry coding, missing clinical variables and incomplete verification limit interpretation. Chiche assembled 49 confirmed cases through registry replies and additional centre ascertainment; subtracting 49 from 64 does not establish 15 miscoded cases. The UNOS analysis also lacked lesion number, size and complete case-level pathology review. Preserve these limitations without inventing a measured misclassification rate.

changes.old: This is the commonest real decision and no document answers it. The Italian guideline recommends biopsy specifically to identify exon 3 and sonic hedgehog adenomas (its PICO 9) and simultaneously keeps 5 cm as the resection trigger (its PICO 11), without specifying which governs when they disagree. The review of the WHO 6th-edition classification states that exon 3 adenomas are resected whatever their size, but cites no cohort. EASL's rule is explicitly size-first and subtype-blind above the threshold. The molecular data support subtype in both directions — 2 of 14 women with an at-risk profile under 5 cm transformed against 1 of 101 without — but on two events. Write the precedence rule down, with the proviso that it will be applied to a subtype assignment that is often made without sequencing.
changes.new: Imaging subtype and a confirmed molecular alteration are different findings. EASL recommends resection for proven beta-catenin mutation irrespective of size; ACG particularly identifies exon 3 risk, and AISF PICO 11 also recognizes proven beta-catenin mutation as an independent resection trigger. The programme should specify how molecular confirmation, exon/codon and operative risk inform this assessment rather than state a blanket size-only rule.

changes.old: NANETS says biopsy is not routinely necessary before deciding to observe a sub-centimetre lesion with a characteristic imaging phenotype. ENETS 2023, read in full, says a suspected nonfunctioning tumour under 2 cm with positive receptor imaging should be confirmed histologically or cytologically where possible (level 3, grade B). The 2025 MEN1 recommendations find no role for routine EUS-guided biopsy in that syndrome. There is no outcome evidence separating the three, and both options carry a real cost: EUS-FNA cytology called 71% of histological G2 tumours G1, while two thirds of ASPEN's surveillance arm had no evaluable histology at all. The programme needs one answer, and a stated reason.

changes.source_locator: Full_Text_Review_2026-10-31/Analyst_B/batches/B20_pnet_roadmap/reviews/R7/36434154.md; Chan 2023 pp552–554, Tables2–4 and limitations
changes.old: Do not use this to decide an operation on a localised primary. Both cohorts were metastatic or unresectable disease; only 39% and 36% of patients had pancreatic primaries and no pancreas-specific subgroup is reported in either; two of the three validation centres supplied the original derivation data, so this is partly a re-analysis rather than external validation; and treatment was not modelled in either paper, which matters because receptor-positive, FDG-negative disease is precisely the eligibility criterion for peptide receptor radionuclide therapy, so part of the P1 advantage is access to an effective drug. The 5-point scale has never been shown to be prognostic level by level - every published analysis collapses it to three categories, and several sub-grades contained a single patient. The score carries no treatment threshold.
changes.new: Do not use NETPET alone to decide an operation on a localized primary. The cohorts involved metastatic or unresectable disease, with only 39% and 36% pancreatic primaries and no pancreas-specific analysis. The validation centres had published earlier series, but patient overlap with those series is unquantified. Treatment was not adjusted for. SSTR-positive disease across P1–P4 may be eligible for PRRT; FDG positivity does not by itself exclude it, so treatment access cannot be attributed only to P1. These data support prognosis, not a validated treatment threshold or a localized-primary resection rule.

changes.source_locator: Full_Text_Review_2026-10-31/Analyst_B/batches/B20_pnet_roadmap/reviews/R7/36434154.md; Chan 2023 pp552–554, Tables2–4 and limitations
changes.old: The combined-PET score is now better supported and still inapplicable here. In the 319-patient three-centre cohort it independently predicted overall survival (HR 2.376, 1.682-3.357, p<0.001) and time to progression, with inter-rater kappa 0.8 - but histological grade was independently prognostic alongside it (HR 1.615, 1.192-2.187, p=0.002), so the claim in the first draft that the score outperformed pathological grading holds only in the 62-patient derivation cohort where grade was non-significant and no multivariable model was fitted. Both cohorts were metastatic or unresectable disease; only 39% and 36% of patients had pancreatic primaries and neither paper reports a pancreatic subgroup; two of the three validation centres supplied the derivation data; and treatment was not modelled, which matters because receptor-positive, FDG-negative disease is the eligibility criterion for radionuclide therapy. The 5-point scale has never been validated level by level and carries no treatment threshold. The SNMMI/EANM standard says FDG positivity predicts progression more strongly than grade and that the combination can direct a biopsy to the worst lesion, and stops there. Applying any of it to a 1.5 cm primary is an extrapolation with no outcome data behind it either way.
changes.new: NETPET and histological grade were independently prognostic in the 319-patient metastatic GEP-NEN validation cohort. This does not establish superiority over pathology or determine treatment for a small localized primary. The study did not adjust for treatment; PRRT eligibility can extend to SSTR-positive P1–P4 disease rather than requiring FDG negativity. Centres had earlier published series, but patient overlap is unquantified. Dual-tracer imaging may help identify a higher-risk biopsy target in selected patients; document how the result would change care.

changes.source_locator: Full_Text_Review_2026-10-31/Analyst_B/batches/B20_pnet_roadmap/reviews/R7/36434154.md; Chan 2023 pp552–554, Tables2–4 and limitations
changes.old: FDG positivity is not rare in G1 and G2 disease and predicts progression and prognosis more strongly than grade on the SNMMI/EANM standard's own reading, and the combined score independently predicted survival in a 319-patient cohort. But both score cohorts were metastatic or unresectable, only about a third of patients had pancreatic primaries, treatment was not modelled, and the score carries no treatment threshold. If the pair is obtained and nothing is done differently, it is a cost; if something is done differently, the programme is acting beyond any published evidence and should say so and record it.
changes.new: The dual-tracer score is prognostic in metastatic or unresectable GEP-NEN, with only about a third pancreatic primaries and no validated threshold for treating a localized primary. Treatment was not adjusted for; SSTR-positive P1–P4 patients may receive PRRT. Define the selected clinical question, biopsy implications and intended management change before adding FDG imaging.

changes.old: In 319 patients with metastatic GEP-NEN the NETPET score independently predicted overall survival and time to progression alongside histological grade, but two of the three contributing centres supplied the original derivation data, treatment was not adjusted for, and only a third of the cohort had pancreatic primaries.
changes.new: In 319 patients with metastatic GEP-NEN, NETPET and histological grade independently predicted overall survival and time to progression. changes.source_locator: Full_Text_Review_2026-10-31/Analyst_A_Continuation_2026-11-01/batches/B26_residual_sources/42456089.md; original PMC13374715 author-manuscript Methods, Results, Tables1–2 and Discussion
changes.old: RTOG 0848 randomised the addition of fluoropyrimidine-based chemoradiation after adjuvant gemcitabine-based chemotherapy in resected pancreatic head cancer. Patients with node-negative disease had longer overall and disease-free survival with the addition; patients with node-positive disease did not.
changes.new: RTOG 0848 randomized 354 patients without recurrence after five chemotherapy cycles. From this randomization, overall survival was not significantly improved (HR 0.96, 90% CI 0.79–1.18), nor was final-report disease-free survival (HR 0.82, 95% CI 0.65–1.03; two-sided P=.089). Significant nodal-status interactions and favorable node-negative results support an individualized discussion, not routine treatment of every resected patient.

changes.source_locator: Full_Text_Review_2026-10-31/Analyst_A_Continuation_2026-11-01/batches/B26_residual_sources/42456089.md; original PMC13374715 author-manuscript Methods, Results, Tables1–2 and Discussion
changes.old: Do not extend this to node-positive disease — in RTOG 0848 chemoradiation did not improve overall or disease-free survival in that group, which is the opposite of the intuition. The benefit was seen in patients who received single-agent gemcitabine as their systemic therapy, so it does not transfer to a patient who had mFOLFIRINOX, and no study has shown superiority of chemoradiation before versus after chemotherapy in the adjuvant setting.
changes.new: None of the patients received FOLFIRINOX: 67% received gemcitabine alone, 28% gemcitabine/erlotinib and 5% other gemcitabine combinations. Benefit after modern chemotherapy is unestablished. Only ten patients were both node-negative and margin-positive, so margin-specific inference is inadequate. SBRT substitution is unestablished.

changes.source_locator: Full_Text_Review_2026-10-31/Analyst_A_Continuation_2026-11-01/batches/B26_residual_sources/42456089.md; original PMC13374715 author-manuscript Methods, Results, Tables1–2 and Discussion
changes.old: Downgraded from C to D: the RTOG 0848 primary publication was not retrieved or read in full for this depot, and the result is carried only in the NCCN discussion text supplied to this page. Adjuvant chemoradiation remains a controversial topic in resected pancreatic cancer, and NCCN warns that RTOG 9704 cannot be compared directly with CONKO-001, ESPAC-1 or ESPAC-3 because of differences in design, imaging timing and patient characteristics. The margin-status subset analyses are retrospective and carried in the same extraction: pooled analyses report benefit in both R0 and R1 subsets, with a relative risk of 0.52 (95% CI 0.36–0.74, P<.001) in one R1 analysis and a non-significant hazard ratio of 0.72 (0.47–1.10) in a four-study meta-analysis. None of these figures has been checked against a primary report.
changes.new: The final primary report is now available. Grade-3 toxicity was greater with chemoradiation (38% versus 19%); grade-4/5 toxicity did not significantly differ. The main clinical text, tables and figure captions were reviewed in the continuation; figure pixels, the separate supplement and protocol were not. The earlier abstract’s one-sided DFS formulation should not replace the final nonsignificant two-sided result.

changes.source_locator: Full_Text_Review_2026-10-31/Analyst_A_Continuation_2026-11-01/batches/B26_residual_sources/42456089.md; original PMC13374715 author-manuscript Methods, Results, Tables1–2 and Discussion
changes.old: The trial's node-positive subgroup showed no improvement in overall or disease-free survival. changes.new: The overall primary result was negative and the node-positive subgroup did not show benefit. A subgroup result does not establish a universal prohibition for every clinical context. The node-negative signal also requires caution after modern chemotherapy.

changes.new: Resolved to the primary NRG Oncology/RTOG 0848 report, PMID42456089, DOI10.1200/JCO-25-02520.
